An .npz is opened and only the members that actually hold a pickle are examined: a numpy array of dtype object stores its contents as a pickle, which is how a payload hides in what looks like a numeric archive. A file with no such member is reported as not applicable rather than as clean, because nothing was examined.

If the scan cannot run at all, no verdict is written and the assessment simply has no file-security axis. A missing scan reads as "not scanned", never as safe.

docs.title: What this path cannot do
docs.text: Two things, by construction. It has no model card, so the G7 checks that ask about training data, intended use and evaluation report as gaps — accurately, since the file says nothing about them. And it describes one file: a model split into shards is currently scanned a shard at a time.

docs.title: Scanning a published dataset
docs.text:
Research data is published where the paper put it, which for a great deal of science is a repository like Figshare rather than a model hub. Hand --model the item instead of a HuggingFace id:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project cell-imaging-data --version 1.0.0 \
  --model "https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Title/33412285" \
  --usage product --generate-only

The page URL, the DOI, or the item number all work. To read a specific version rather than the latest, give the URL or DOI that names it (.../33412285/2, 10.6084/m9.figshare.33413521.v1). No account and no opt-in image are needed: the public item endpoint answers without authentication, and the mapping ships in the base image.

The item becomes a CycloneDX data component carrying its licence, its DOI, its authors, and an MD5 digest per file. A licence the item states as one BomLens can place (the Creative Commons deeds, MIT, Apache 2.0, the GPLs, CC0) becomes an SPDX id; anything else is kept verbatim rather than guessed at. --usage applies here as it does to a model: a non-commercial deed reads differently for internal research than for something you ship.

An institutional DOI that does not carry "figshare" (10.25916/sut.33412285.v1) cannot be told apart from any other DOI, so give the item URL for those. A private, embargoed or withdrawn item cannot be read without an account, and is reported as an error rather than described as a dataset with no licence.

A dataset on HuggingFace is scanned the same way, also in the base image with no account. Give it as datasets/<owner>/<name>, as https://huggingface.co/datasets/<owner>/<name> (anything after the name, such as /tree/main, is ignored), or as hf:<owner>/<name>. A bare owner/name stays a model id, because the hub uses the same form for both, so the prefix or the address is what marks a dataset:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project tulu --version 1.0 \
  --model datasets/allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture --generate-only

The dataset becomes the SBOM's root data component with its licence, the hub revision it was read at (bomlens:dataset:revision) and a SHA-256 digest per file. The datasets its card lists under source_datasets are traced the same way as the datasets a model card names (same AIBOM_DATASET_DEPTH and AIBOM_DATASET_MAX_LOOKUPS limits), appear as rows under it in Models & datasets, and their risk verdicts reach the root. A gated or private dataset needs HF_TOKEN, and a dataset that cannot be read is reported as an error rather than written as an empty SBOM.

Deliverables: notice, ML-BOM (CycloneDX 1.7), risk report, conformance check.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
In the web UI, an AI/ML SBOM adds two sections to the left rail.

Models & datasets — each model card's identifier, architecture, task, license, supplier and integrity, a four-axis disclosure panel (weights / architecture / training data / training process, as documented in the BOM), and a table of the datasets the model references with each one's license, content digest and upstream. A traced source appears as its own row, indented under the dataset it was traced from, with its own grade and license, so the dataset and the source it inherits terms from read side by side.

Conformance — for an AI-model SBOM this section adds the G7 minimum-element checks (all advisory), grouped by the seven G7 clusters, alongside the base format-conformance checks. Each element shows what it is and how to satisfy it. The next section explains what the numbers and badges mean.

The same data is in the artifacts: the ML-BOM (_bom.json, CycloneDX 1.7) and the conformance check report (_conformance.*).

docs.title: The SPDX 3.0.1 AI document
docs.text:
Every AI model and dataset scan also writes the result as an SPDX 3.0.1 document with the AI and Dataset profiles, {Project}_{Version}_bom.spdx3.json, next to the CycloneDX ML-BOM. The CycloneDX file stays the primary record; the SPDX document is built from it, plus whatever the model's publisher declares.

A scan can fill what it reads: the model's name, revision, download address, publisher on the hub, licence, architecture, limitations and weight files with their digests; each dataset's address, licence and data type where its card says; the base models and the datasets the card names. It cannot know when the model was released, who made it, which datasets trained it and which only tested it, or the revision of the base model it started from. SPDX 3.0.1 makes several of these required and gives them no "unknown" value, so until they are declared the document is a draft: it says so in its comment, and {Project}_{Version}_spdx3-check.md lists each open field.

To fill them, edit the empty declaration the scan writes, {Project}_{Version}_ai-declaration.template.json, and scan again with it:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project my-llm --version 1.0 \
  --model "acme/support-adapter" --ai-declare my-llm_1.0_ai-declaration.template.json --generate-only

Most declared values go into the SPDX document only, each marked as declared. The exceptions are the service the model runs in and the model's input and output kinds, training compute and adversarial testing, which also reach the CycloneDX SBOM (see The service a model runs in). A declaration that names a dataset or base model the scan did not find, a value outside a field's list, or a date not written as YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ is refused with the reasons. Some fields are a judgement the tool never makes for you: whether the model uses sensitive personal information, its safety risk level, and its autonomy. The check lists them as needing a decision, and leaving them empty is allowed. model.license (a HuggingFace licence tag or an SPDX licence id) gives the model's own licence when the scan read none, or only other; one that differs from the licence the scan read is listed for review, and the scan's is kept. It is written as an SPDX expression only when it is a hub tag that names exactly one SPDX licence, or a LicenseRef-; anything else is kept in words, with NoAssertionLicense as the expression.

In the web UI there is no file to edit: Models & datasets shows the document's state and a Fill in empty fields button that asks for the open fields one step at a time and saves them as the declaration (see the web UI reference). The saved declaration is the same {Project}_{Version}_ai-declaration.json file, so a re-scan applies it again, from the CLI as well.

A model being prepared for release has no repository or file to scan, so it can be described from the declaration alone: give --ai-declare <file> without --model or --model-file, or pick Enter model information on the web UI's New scan screen, which asks the same questions and starts the scan with the answers.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project support-bot --version 1.0 \
  --ai-declare support-bot-declaration.json --generate-only

The model becomes the SBOM's subject under the project name and version, marked bomlens:origin=declared-input. The base models listed in model.baseModels[].ref and the datasets in datasets[].ref (huggingface:<owner>/<name>) are read from the hub by id, so their lineage, licences and traced sources are the same as in a model scan, and datasets[].local holds data the hub does not have. The risk assessment, the G7 check and this document follow as usual. No hub supplies the download address and supplier, so the document stays a draft until they are declared.

Here the whole SBOM is the publisher's statement, so two declared values enter it. The names in document.createdBy become the SBOM author when --sbom-author is not given, marked bomlens:sbom-author-source=declaration. The model's own licence, model.license, is the other: the risk assessment judges the model on it, and an ancestor under the same terms is not flagged as a mismatch. Without it the model has no licence and its verdict reads review. It enters the SBOM when the scan runs, so a licence changed later with Fill in empty fields is listed for review until the model is scanned again.

A dataset's card often lists no sources, so the scan cannot trace them. The declaration can name them for each dataset (sources[], and a "Where this data came from" row in the web UI's questions). A source given by its HuggingFace id is read from the hub on the next scan, before the risk assessment, so its recorded licence counts in the dataset's verdict just as a traced source's does. A source known only by name is written to the SPDX 3.0.1 document with the licence you give, marked as declared and not verified, and does not change the verdict. A declaration the converter refuses is not applied here either. A dataset the model card names (or the dataset a scan describes) with no source on record anywhere is listed in the check for review.

Two rules apply. A value that is not in the scan and not declared is left out rather than estimated, and a base model is written by its id and licence only, so nothing the publisher declares about the model is copied onto it. --no-spdx3 skips the document.

docs.title: The service a model runs in
docs.text:
A model card describes the model. The G7 checklist also asks about the system around it: the system's name, maker and version, how data flows through it, what it does with that data, its input and output, and the field it is meant for. None of that is in a model card or a weight file, so without help those elements stay review items. When you run the model inside an app or an API, the declaration can describe that service, and BomLens writes it into both documents. The EU AI Act's technical documentation (Annex IV, point 1) and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (MAP 1.1, the intended purpose and context of use) ask for the same kind of description. They are named here only as context; declaring a service does not show that a system meets either.

In the declaration file the service is a top-level service object:

"service": {
  "name": "Acme Support Assistant",
  "packageVersion": "2.3.0",
  "downloadLocation": "https://support.acme.example/assistant",
  "suppliedBy": {"type": "Organization", "name": "Acme Corp"},
  "releaseTime": "2025-06-01T00:00:00Z",
  "informationAboutApplication": "Answers customer support questions in the web chat.",
  "domain": ["customer support"],
  "autonomyType": "no",
  "inputModality": ["text"],
  "outputModality": ["text"],
  "dataFlows": [
    {"flow": "inbound", "classification": "personal data",
     "description": "Customer questions typed in the chat window.",
     "source": ["https://support.acme.example/chat"]}
  ],
  "standardCompliance": ["ISO/IEC 42001:2023"],
  "disclosureUrl": "https://support.acme.example/ai-disclosure"
}

SPDX requires the first five keys of a service, and the document stays a draft until they are given; the rest are optional. autonomyType answers whether a person is involved in the AI's decisions: no means a person is involved, yes that it acts fully automatically, and noAssertion that you do not know. Every key and allowed value is listed in the artifacts reference. In the web UI the same questions form the optional Service step of Fill in empty fields and of Enter model information.

The SPDX 3.0.1 document writes the service as an ai_AIPackage with the purpose application that depends on the model at runtime; the model stays the document's root. The scan also writes the service into the CycloneDX SBOM, in a step that runs after the declared dataset sources are read and before the risk assessment and the G7 checks. The service goes into services[] with its data flows as data[], its dependency on the model into dependencies[], and each standard it names into declarations.claims[]. Each of these is marked bomlens:origin=declared-input, and a claim's reasoning says it is the publisher's declaration, not verified by BomLens.

With a service declared, the G7 system-level elements read from it: the system name, producer and version when the SBOM's root does not already give them, and the system data flow, data usage (the description of a data flow), input/output properties and intended application area. An element met this way reads "present (publisher's declaration, not verified by BomLens)", and the web UI gives it a "Publisher's declaration" badge. BomLens records what you state; it does not check that the service behaves that way. An SBOM from another tool counts too when its services carry CycloneDX data (serviceData) entries: a flow direction meets the data flow element and a description meets data usage, and both read as plainly present. A security standard named in standardCompliance does not meet the security compliance element, which stays a review item.

The CycloneDX SBOM changes only when a scan runs. A service saved in the web UI after the scan goes into the SPDX document at once, but reaches the CycloneDX SBOM and the G7 checks only with the next scan. Until then the SPDX check reports service.state as pendingScan, and the band on Models & datasets offers a re-scan. A declaration passed with --ai-declare is applied in the same run.

docs.title: External AI models
docs.text: A service often calls models it does not run itself, such as a hosted translation or embedding API. List them under service.externalModels[], each with a key and a name, and optionally suppliedBy, packageVersion and endpoint. They are recorded by identity only: a software_Package with the purpose model in the SPDX document, and a service of its own in CycloneDX services[] that the declared service depends on. BomLens reads nothing about them; the risk assessment does not judge them, and the G7 checks do not count them as models.

docs.title: Values for regulatory filings
docs.text:
Rules for large general-purpose models ask for figures no model card holds. The declaration's model takes three of them:

  • trainingComputeFlops, the compute used to train the model in floating-point operations, written as a decimal string such as "3.2e24", with trainingComputeBasis saying how it was counted. The EU AI Act asks for the training compute in the technical documentation of a general-purpose AI model (Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(d)) and uses it in Article 51(2) to presume high-impact capabilities. The Korean AI Basic Act enforcement decree, Article 24, also refers to training compute.
  • adversarialTesting (yes, no or noAssertion), whether adversarial testing such as red-teaming was done. Article 55(1)(a) of the EU AI Act asks providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk to conduct and document it.

The articles are named so you know why the fields exist. BomLens does not compare a figure with a threshold or decide whether a rule applies to your model, and filling these fields does not make a model compliant with any of them.

The model also takes inputModality and outputModality (text, image, audio, video, timeseries, structured, code, other). All five values go into the SPDX document and onto the model component of the CycloneDX SBOM: the three regulatory values as bomlens:regulatory:* properties, and the input and output kinds as formats in modelCard.modelParameters. Where the scan already recorded inputs or outputs there, the scanned values are kept. A bomlens:declared property names each location filled from the declaration.

docs.title: Older BomLens versions
docs.text: BomLens v1.13 and earlier do not know these keys. They refuse a declaration that has a service, or one of the new model keys, with "unknown key(s)" rather than dropping the values without a word; read such a file with a version that has them, or remove the keys. The SPDX 2.3 export and --diff do not carry services: the SPDX 2.3 copy is converted from the components of the CycloneDX SBOM, and --diff compares models and components.

docs.title: Reading the conformance check report
docs.text:
The G7 block leads with a headline such as "N / 41 present". The denominator counts only the checks that have an automated source (41 of the 51), so the number states what the tool could verify on its own. The 10 review-only elements appear next to it as a separate "need review" count, and any automated check that found nothing is counted as advisory. Four of the ten, the system data flow, data usage, input/output properties and application area, leave the review count and join the denominator once the SBOM holds a value for them, which a declared service supplies.

Each check has one of three statuses. Pass means the element is present in the ML-BOM. Warn means it is missing or could not be confirmed; the review-only elements always show this status, labeled as requiring human review. Fail does not occur for G7 checks in practice: every G7 element is advisory, so a missing one never fails the SBOM as a whole. An overall fail verdict can only come from the base format checks, the required CycloneDX ones.

Some rows read "not applicable" instead, with a count of their own in the summary. Those are checks the document gives nothing to judge: a coverage percentage over zero components, or dependency relationships in a document whose only subject is the model itself. They leave both sides of the fraction rather than counting as met, because crediting them would put a card that declares less above one that declares its datasets and is measured on them. They are not review items either — a reviewer has nothing to look at. A model card that names its training datasets therefore has more checks actually measured, and a smaller denominator is not a better result.

A source badge on each row says where a satisfied value comes from:

  • Auto (22 checks): read directly from a field of the ML-BOM.
  • Inferred (15): derived from signals in the BOM rather than a single dedicated field.
  • Declared (8): present only when a person or a manifest supplied the value. Four of them (the system data flow, data usage, input/output properties and application area) show as review needed until the SBOM holds a value. A pass that comes from the publisher's declaration says so in its detail.
  • Review needed (6, or 10 with the four above): no automated source exists; a person has to confirm it.

The same result ships in three formats: {Project}_{Version}_conformance.json for machines (CI gates, diffing), _conformance.md as a readable table, and _conformance.html as a visual summary. Each format also carries the regulatory crosswalk; in JSON it is the regulatoryCrosswalk object, present only when at least one mapped check was evaluated.

The report shows how to close a gap, not only that one exists. Every advisory element with an automated source that is still absent carries a CycloneDX fragment and a link to the authoritative documentation — in the HTML, behind the "Evidence / how to fill" cell on that row; in the Markdown, gathered under "How to fill the gaps". Passing and review-only elements are left out, so a well-documented model shows none of this.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
A concrete run helps read the rest. FINAL-Bench/Aether-7B-5Attn is a foundation model published on HuggingFace under Apache-2.0 with its weights, architecture, training data and training process all disclosed, so it shows what a well-documented card produces.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project Aether-7B-5Attn --version 1.0 \
  --model "FINAL-Bench/Aether-7B-5Attn" --generate-only

A scan on 2026-10-23 (model revision da711bdb) reports result=pass with 30 of 41 G7 elements present. The figures follow the model card, so a later revision can give different ones. In the Models cluster 12 of 14 checks pass; the SBOM has no model timestamp and no model description. The disclosure panel reads open on every axis:

Axis Value Weights open-weight Architecture open-architecture Training data open-data Training process open-training

Because the card lists its datasets, BomLens looks up all seven the model was trained on (FineWeb-Edu, the SmolLM corpus, FineMath, open-web-math, an OpenCoder code corpus, and two Korean sets from HAERAE-HUB) and records what each one declares. Eight of the ten Dataset-properties elements come back present. The two that remain are the statistical properties of the data and whether it contains personal or copyrighted material; neither can be read from a repository, so the report asks a person rather than guessing.

The lookup is what makes the next part visible. Four of the seven datasets carry a license: odc-by on FineWeb-Edu, FineMath and the SmolLM corpus, and MIT on the OpenCoder corpus. The other three declare none at all: both HAERAE-HUB sets and open-web-math. Counting dataset names would have called this model's training data fully open. Reading the datasets shows a model published under Apache-2.0 whose training corpus is, in part, of unstated license. That is not a finding the tool judges; it is the one a reviewer needs before release, and it only appears once each dataset is looked up.

A report from the same command is here to open as-is: the conformance check report for the base model. It comes from the same 2026-10-23 run as the figures above. It opens with the same G7 rollup the AI compliance profile carries in JSON and Markdown. Add --lang ko for the same reports in Korean; the SBOM and the JSON reports stay English either way.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
A report is not a finished review. Some elements a tool can fill; others only a person can.

  1. Fill the elements that have an automated source but came back empty, then scan again. The shape that satisfies each one sits on its own row in the report.
  2. Answer the 10 review-only elements yourself: things like training-data sensitivity or the intended application area, which no model card field can prove. If the model runs in a service, declaring it fills four of them (see The service a model runs in).
  3. Check separately what this tool does not look at, such as training dataset licensing and personal data.

If you are preparing a model for release inside a company, the approval steps and the pre-release checks live alongside this: see Releasing an AI model in the SK Telecom open source guide.

docs.title: The G7 checklist
docs.text:
"G7 Software Bill of Materials for AI — Minimum Elements" is a guideline published in May 2026 under the G7, led by Germany's BSI and Italy's ACN. It defines 50 minimum elements, grouped into seven clusters, that an SBOM for an AI model should carry: who made the model, what it is, what data it was trained on, how it is secured, and how it performs. It is a non-binding recommendation, not a regulation.

It still matters for regulation. The EU AI Act's high-risk and transparency obligations apply from 2 August 2026, and the technical documentation its Annex IV asks for overlaps substantially with the G7 clusters. What the conformance check report gives you is visibility: element by element, it shows what your model's documentation already covers and what a person still has to supply — a concrete way to prepare, not a compliance verdict (see Limits for what it does not certify).

BomLens shows the 50 elements as 51 checks. Model openness (whether weights, architecture, training data and training process are disclosed) is one facet of the Model license element in the G7 text, but it is worth seeing on its own, so it gets a separate row.

Cluster Checks Of which need human review Metadata 10 0 System-level properties 9 4 (0 when a service fills them) Models 14 0 Dataset properties 10 2 Infrastructure 2 0 Security properties 4 3 Key performance indicators 2 1

Ten elements have no automated source, such as the intended application area or dataset sensitivity, which no model-card field can prove. BomLens lists them as requiring human review instead of guessing. The four system-level ones (data flow, data usage, input/output properties and application area) are read from CycloneDX services[]: all four from a declared service, and data flow and data usage also from the services of another tool's SBOM. Once the SBOM holds a value for one, it stops counting as a review item.

docs.title: Regulatory crosswalk
docs.text:
The conformance check report links each check that maps to a regulation to the specific documentation obligation it touches. It answers a reviewer's question: when a check comes back short, which regulatory requirement does that gap concern? The reference sits under the requirement it belongs to in the check tables, and a crosswalk section above the detail rolls the coverage up — one row per framework, counting how many mapped checks are present, a gap, or review-only.

Two frameworks cover every analyzed SBOM, AI or not:

  • EU Cyber Resilience Act — via BSI TR-03183-2, the German technical guideline written for CRA compliance and the most detailed public SBOM field specification (the CRA itself names no data fields). TR-03183-2 is a national guideline, and the European harmonized standard that will carry the binding wording is still a draft.
  • US SBOM minimum elements — the 17 data fields and 6 practices of the 2026 minimum elements, published by CISA, the NSA and the FBI with fifteen international partners and replacing the NTIA elements of 2021. Federal SBOM collection has since been narrowed to agency-level, risk-based decisions, but the fields remain the practical baseline that individual agencies ask for.

The crosswalk above covers SBOM data fields only. For the broader CRA readiness process those fields sit inside — governance, vulnerability handling, the technical file, security updates — see the community-maintained OpenChain CRA Compliance Requirements & Checklist.

For an AI SBOM, two more frameworks map onto the G7 elements:

  • EU AI Act — the technical-documentation sections of Annex IV (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 11(1)).
  • AI Framework Act (Korea) — the Act's articles on transparency (제31조), safety and risk management (제32조), high-impact AI (제33·34조), and impact assessment (제35조). The Act sets framework-level duties, so these links are coarser than the EU ones.

The crosswalk is a preparation aid, not a compliance verdict (see Limits). Each mapping carries the interpretive basis for the link so a person can judge it, and the crosswalk never changes a check's status or the overall result — it only regroups findings the checks already produced.

The mapping lives in docker/lib/regulation-crosswalk.json, keyed by check id — the G7 element ids for the AI checks and the plain CycloneDX check ids for the base format checks. It is deliberately conservative: only checks with a defensible correspondence are mapped. Today that is 74 check ids with 84 links across the four frameworks, since one check can point at more than one framework. A test validates every mapped id against the registry so the crosswalk cannot drift silently when a check is renamed.

docs.title: AI compliance profile
docs.text: For an AI SBOM, BomLens also writes a one-page AI compliance profile (_ai-profile.{json,md,html}) that gathers into one place what otherwise lives across separate artifacts: the G7 status by cluster, the regulatory crosswalk, and the components whose license is flagged for review (AI behavioral-use or non-commercial). It runs no scan and makes no compliance determination — it regroups findings the pipeline already produced, so a reviewer can read the whole picture at a glance. It is written for the AI-model (--model) and supplier-SBOM (--analyze) paths, and is a no-op for a plain (non-AI) SBOM.

docs.title: Model risk assessment
docs.text:
The AI compliance profile also carries a usability verdict per model, answering the question a development team asks first: can we use this model, and under what conditions? Each model — and each dataset entry — is assessed on the axes the pipeline has evidence for and given one of four verdicts.

Verdict Meaning ok Only known unrestricted signals — for example a permissive license. conditional Usable when the listed conditions are met — for example the Llama community license's user threshold and naming rule, or a copyleft license's notice duties. caution A known blocking signal — for example a non-commercial or research-only license. review The tool cannot judge: an unrecognized license, a missing license, or a dataset that could not be read. A person has to look.

The file-security axis reads the scan results Hugging Face itself runs over every repository — ClamAV for malware and picklescan for executable pickle imports, per file. BomLens reads them through the metadata API without downloading a single file, records the worst status with the flagged file names, and notes whether the weights use a pickle-family format (which can execute code on load) or a safe one such as safetensors. A model whose scan is still pending reads review, not safe. Set ENRICH_HF_SECURITY=false to skip the lookup.

The license verdict comes from a curated registry (docker/lib/ai-risk-knowledge.json) covering the complete Hugging Face license tag list. Each entry records whether commercial use, redistribution and derivatives are allowed, the conditions that apply, and a link to the license text; the profile prints the summary and the conditions next to the verdict, so the grounds travel with the judgement. A license the registry does not know falls to review — it is never guessed. A model's overall verdict is the worst across its assessed axes, and an axis nothing evaluated shows as not assessed rather than being read as safe.

Two further checks deepen the license verdict. For a model tagged other, BomLens reads the repository's LICENSE file (one small text file — still no weight download) and searches it for restrictive wording such as non-commercial, research-only or no-derivatives clauses; a match is quoted verbatim next to the verdict, so the report says "review needed because of this sentence" rather than only "unclassified". No match still reads review — a pattern miss proves nothing. And for a fine-tuned model, BomLens walks the declared base-model chain (up to five ancestors) and compares licenses: when an ancestor carries a license whose conditions extend to derivatives (Llama, Gemma, the RAIL family, non-commercial CC) but the model itself declares something else, the mismatch is flagged as a caution — a common mislabeling on the hub that a tag-only check cannot see.

The datasets axis rolls the referenced datasets up into the model's verdict. Each dataset entry is judged on its own license and on its declared risk markers: a publisher tag such as pii (personally identifiable information) or not-for-all-audiences, and an access restriction (gated or private repository). The model takes the worst dataset verdict, with the offending datasets named. These markers are the publisher's own declarations — their absence proves nothing, so they only ever raise a verdict, never clear one.

A dataset's traced sources are judged the same way and carried into the dataset's own verdict: the strictest verdict anywhere below a dataset decides it, and the reason names the source and its license (for example source org/nc: cc-by-nc-4.0 (caution)). A source that could not be read, declares no license, or is named only in words reads review, and so does a dataset whose sources lie past the depth limit, since those were not read. The rule reads recorded licenses and nothing else; whether a source's owner relicensed the derived data on other terms is not something it can see.

The verdict can be tailored to how you will actually use the model. Pass --usage with one of internal (in-house review and research), product (shipping in a product or service), redistribute (fine-tuning and redistribution) or outputs-only (using only what the model generates), and only the license conditions that bind that scenario decide the verdict — a non-commercial model, for example, reads conditional for internal research but caution for product use. The report always states which scenario it judged for; without --usage every condition counts.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project my-llm --version 1.0 \
  --model "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" --usage product --generate-only

The verdicts are guidance, not legal advice, and every report that prints them says so. They gather what a reviewer needs — the terms, the sources, the unknowns — so the final decision is made by a person with the evidence in one place.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A model the tool cannot read produces no SBOM at all. The generator fills the card with generic defaults when a fetch fails, so BomLens checks its log and refuses the run rather than handing back an inventory of placeholders that would read as a pass.
  • The result is only as complete as the HuggingFace model card. A sparse card yields a sparse ML-BOM, and the G7 checks reflect what the card documents — not an audit of the model.
  • Dataset entries record what a dataset declares about itself. The verdict now shows when a source's recorded terms are stricter than the derived dataset's, but whether the declared license is the right one, and whether the source was relicensed for the derived use, is a judgement the report leaves to a reviewer. Sources a card does not name cannot be traced.
  • A compound SPDX license expression (MIT OR Apache-2.0) is assessed as a whole rather than by resolving the choice, so a dual-licensed model can read review where either option alone would be ok. The direction is deliberately cautious — it never under-warns — but it may over-flag; the report names the exact expression so a reviewer can confirm.
  • The conformance check report does not certify compliance with the EU AI Act, the Korean AI Framework Act, or any other regulation. It makes documentation gaps visible so a person can close them.
  • It fetches metadata over the network, so offline use is not supported. Private and gated models need HF_TOKEN (see Private and gated models).
  • The model id must be org/model. A collection name or a full URL will not resolve.

Related: Pipeline by input type | Web UI reference | CLI reference

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: An open-source compliance manager receives deliverables from many teams in different forms. This guide shows how to produce the same four deliverables for each of seven input forms. (An AI model differs slightly — an ML-BOM and no security report; see Scenario 7.)

docs.title: The four deliverables
docs.text:
Deliverable File Meaning Open-source notice {Project}_{Version}_NOTICE.{txt,html} the notice that satisfies license obligations SBOM {Project}_{Version}_bom.json CycloneDX 1.6 component inventory (1.7 with --spec-version 1.7) Open-source risk report {Project}_{Version}_risk-report.{md,html} aggregated license + vulnerability risk (with deadlines) Conformance check report {Project}_{Version}_conformance.{json,md,html} whether the SBOM meets the submission quality criteria, and what is missing

The conformance check report's file is always produced, but the web UI only shows it as a dedicated pass/fail screen when the input being checked is a supplied SBOM (the --analyze path); a self-generated SBOM grading itself is not a meaningful pass/fail signal for most of its checks. For a self-generated scan, open the file directly, or feed the output back in with --analyze to see it on screen. See Reading the conformance check report.

For any input form, adding --all --generate-only produces all four at once (they are on by default and are only turned off with --no-report).

docs.title: Common setup
docs.text:
Windows: the commands here are for macOS/Linux. Pick one of the following. See Getting started for installation.

  • Replace ./scripts/scan-sbom.sh with scripts\scan-sbom.bat (needs Git Bash).
  • Under WSL2, run the commands as-is.
  • To work without a command line, double-click scripts\sbom-ui.bat.
# Docker 20.10+ required. Pull the scanner image once (or build it yourself).
docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest   # legacy name sbom-scanner serves the same image

# For convenience, keep the script path in a variable.
SBOM=/path/to/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
$SBOM in every command below is the script path variable from Common setup — if you skipped that step, put the full path to scan-sbom.sh in its place.

Input form Mode Core command (summary) Deliverables GitHub URL SOURCE $SBOM --git <url> --all --generate-only notice, SBOM, risk report, conformance check report Source ZIP SOURCE $SBOM --target app.zip --all --generate-only same Local directory (C/C++) SOURCE cd dir && $SBOM --all --generate-only same Existing SBOM JSON ANALYZE $SBOM --analyze sbom.json --generate-only same, but the SBOM is the converted input rather than freshly generated Yocto build directory ANALYZE $SBOM --target ~/poky/build --generate-only same Build artifact (.jar, .deb, …) BINARY $SBOM --target app.jar --all --generate-only same Installer (.exe, .msi, .dmg) FIRMWARE $SBOM --target installer.exe --all --generate-only same Mobile app (.apk, .ipa) FIRMWARE $SBOM --target app.apk --all --generate-only same Firmware .bin FIRMWARE $SBOM --target dev.bin --firmware --all --generate-only same AI model (HuggingFace) AIBOM $SBOM --model owner/name --generate-only notice, ML-BOM (1.7), risk report (no security) AI model file (GGUF, safetensors, …) MODELFILE $SBOM --model-file ./model.gguf --generate-only notice, ML-BOM (1.7), risk report (no security) Published dataset (Figshare or HuggingFace) DATASET $SBOM --model <item URL or datasets/owner/name> --generate-only notice, ML-BOM (1.7), risk report (no security) Model not yet published (declaration only) AIDECLARE $SBOM --ai-declare declaration.json --generate-only notice, ML-BOM (1.7), risk report (no security), SPDX 3.0.1 AI document

Every command also needs --project <name> --version <version> (see examples below).

C/C++ without a package manager (Conan/vcpkg): add --identify-vendored so open source copied straight into the sources is detected as named components. Strongly recommended for this case — see Scenario 3.

docs.title: Scenario 1 — GitHub URL
docs.text:
A team handed you a GitHub repository. Pass the URL directly, no manual git clone. ($SBOM is defined in Common setup.)

$SBOM --project team1-app --version 1.0.0 \
  --git "https://github.com/docker/getting-started-app" \
  --all --generate-only
  • Specific branch/tag: --branch v1.2.3
  • Private repository: GIT_TOKEN=ghp_xxx $SBOM ... --git https://github.com/org/private ... (the token never appears in logs)
  • A shallow clone (--depth 1) is fetched to a temp directory and analyzed; only the deliverables remain, in a {Project}_{Version}/ subfolder under the current directory.
  • A monorepo with its own examples/, fixtures/, or test-data/ subfolders can pull in components that never ship in the product, because there is no option yet to scope the scan to one subfolder. Point --git at the specific app repository rather than an umbrella repository when that distinction matters — a component list padded with unrelated demo dependencies (and, in the worst case, one of them flagged as malicious by osv.dev when it is really just an unused dev dependency of an unrelated example) undermines the notice and risk report for everyone downstream.

Deliverables: team1-app_1.0.0_NOTICE.{txt,html}, team1-app_1.0.0_bom.json, team1-app_1.0.0_risk-report.{md,html}, team1-app_1.0.0_conformance.{json,md,html}

docs.title: Scenario 2 — Source ZIP
docs.text:
A team handed you the source as a ZIP. Pass the archive directly, no manual extraction.

$SBOM --project team2-app --version 1.0.0 \
  --target "./team2-app.zip" \
  --all --generate-only
  • Supported: .zip, .tar.gz, .tgz, .tar.bz2, .tar.xz, .tar
  • It is extracted to a temp directory after a zip-slip (path-escape) check; a single top-level folder is entered automatically.

Deliverables: notice, SBOM, risk report, conformance check report (four)

docs.title: Scenario 3 — Local C/C++ source directory
docs.text:
A team shared the source via a folder you copied locally (~/project/c-dev). Run from inside the directory.

cd ~/project/c-dev
$SBOM --project team3-dev --version 1.0.0 --all --deep-license --generate-only
  • With a package manager (Conan conanfile.txt / vcpkg vcpkg.json), dependencies resolve and appear in the SBOM.
  • Pure CMake/Make sources have no manager metadata, so the SBOM can be sparse. Enrich first-party license headers with --deep-license (the post-process step runs on the ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-deep-license image, which carries ScanCode and is pulled automatically; when it cannot be pulled, the scan runs on the base image without the license scan, warns, and records the step as skipped (fallback) in the result manifest), and analyze build output (a staging/rootfs with installed libraries) separately with $SBOM --target <build-dir> --all --generate-only (syft). For a full server SBOM workflow (OS rootfs, application, and static-link dependencies as separate layers), see the server SBOM guide. In the web UI, --deep-license is the License scan (ScanCode) toggle in the Result quality group; it scans your own source files (/src), not the declared dependencies, and is slow, so turn it on only when you need per-file license detection.
  • When the source has no package manager (plain Make/CMake) and bundles open source copied straight into the tree — common for embedded and firmware sources — --identify-vendored is strongly recommended. Without it the SBOM stays sparse and misses the bundled libraries; with it they are detected as named components with CPEs, so the risk report can match CVEs. See Identify bundled open source. BomLens also nudges you toward this option automatically when it detects this situation.
  • Even without a package manager, the risk report is still generated, aggregating licenses and vulnerabilities of detected components.

Deliverables: notice, SBOM, risk report, conformance check report (four)

docs.title: Scenario 4 — Existing SBOM JSON
docs.text:
A team handed you an SBOM (JSON). Validate and analyze it even without the source.

$SBOM --project team4-proj --version 2.0.0 \
  --analyze "./team4-sbom.json" \
  --generate-only
  • CycloneDX (JSON or XML) and SPDX (JSON/Tag-Value) are accepted and converted to CycloneDX internally. SPDX RDF/XML is not supported yet.
  • --analyze turns on notice and security automatically, so you do not need --all.
  • A conformance check report (_conformance.{json,md,html}) is also produced, and the first section of the risk report includes the conformance result (whether required fields are present). For what counts as a fail vs. a warn, see Reading the conformance check report in the supplier SBOM guide.

Deliverables: notice, SBOM (converted), risk report, conformance check report

docs.title: Scenario 5 — Yocto build directory
docs.text:
You build an embedded Linux image with Yocto and want to know what shipped in it. Point the scan at the build directory; the build already recorded the answer.

$SBOM --project team5-image --version 1.0.0 \
  --target ~/poky/build \
  --generate-only
  • Configure the build to emit an SBOM — add INHERIT += "create-spdx-3.0" and INHERIT += "vex" to conf/local.conf — and you get the most out of it. Without it, BomLens still reads what the build wrote by default. See Yocto images for the SPDX-version compatibility table and what happens when a build produced no SPDX at all.
  • The image SBOM under tmp/deploy/images/<machine>/ is analyzed — not the build tree, which holds sysroots and native build tools that never ship in the image.
  • The component list is the packages installed in the image, and vulnerabilities carry the verdicts the build itself made (patched by a recipe, judged not applicable, or still open). Only the open ones count as findings.
  • Components get the upstream repository purl for the projects the firmware guide lists. A build that wrote only SPDX 2.2 carries no build verdicts, so with --security its CPEs are matched against the NVD CPE index in the image instead; SPDX 2.2 does not record which CVEs a recipe patched, so these findings can include CVEs the recipe already patched. SPDX 3.0 records it.
  • If several machines or images were built, the newest SBOM is analyzed and every candidate is listed in the log; pass --analyze <file> to choose a different one.
  • In the web UI, pick the folder with the Directory / rootfs input (mount it with --ui --mount ~/poky/build, or use Add folder in the desktop app) — the same detection runs there.
  • For the full behavior and its limits, see the Yocto section of the supplier SBOM guide.

Deliverables: notice, SBOM, risk report, conformance check report

docs.title: Scenario 6 — Firmware binary
docs.text:
A team handed you a built firmware image (dev.bin). Unpack it and identify components.

$SBOM --project team6-fw --version 1.0.0 \
  --target "./dev.bin" --firmware \
  --all --generate-only
  • Firmware analysis needs the opt-in firmware image, which includes GPL tools (unblob, cve-bin-tool, etc.). Set it via SBOM_FIRMWARE_IMAGE, or pull the default (ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-firmware:latest).
  • Recognized extensions (.bin/.img/.squashfs/.ubi/...) are auto-detected even without --firmware, but being explicit is recommended.
  • For behavior and limits, see the firmware analysis guide.

Deliverables: notice, SBOM, risk report, conformance check report (four)

docs.title: Scenario 7 — AI model (HuggingFace)
docs.text:
A team points you at a HuggingFace model instead of code. Generate an ML-BOM from the model id — no source code and no model-weight download.

$SBOM --project bert-base --version 1.0.0 \
  --model "google-bert/bert-base-uncased" \
  --generate-only
  • Needs the opt-in aibom image (ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-aibom:latest), pulled automatically. Set a different tag via SBOM_AIBOM_IMAGE.
  • --model is mutually exclusive with --target/--analyze/--git/--merge.
  • Produces a CycloneDX 1.7 ML-BOM (not 1.6), the notice, and the risk report, plus a G7 minimum-element conformance check. There is no security report — a model has no package CVEs.
  • For the model card, datasets, and G7 details, see the AI model guide.

Deliverables: notice, ML-BOM (CycloneDX 1.7), risk report, G7 conformance

docs.title: When it is a published dataset, not a model
docs.text:
Research data is published where the paper put it, which for a great deal of science is a repository like Figshare rather than a model hub. Hand --model the item instead:

$SBOM --project cell-imaging-data --version 1.0.0 \
  --model "https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Title/33412285" \
  --usage product --generate-only

The page URL, the DOI, or the item number all work, and no account or opt-in image is needed.

A dataset on HuggingFace goes the same way. Give it as datasets/<owner>/<name>, as its https://huggingface.co/datasets/<owner>/<name> address, or as hf:<owner>/<name>. A bare owner/name is read as a model id, because the hub uses the same form for both:

$SBOM --project tulu --version 1.0 \
  --model datasets/allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture --generate-only

For version selection, the licence-to-SPDX mapping, how a private or embargoed item is handled, and how a HuggingFace dataset's sources are traced, see Scanning a published dataset in the AI model guide.

Deliverables: notice, ML-BOM (CycloneDX 1.7), risk report, conformance check

docs.title: When the model has no repository or file yet
docs.text:
A model being prepared for release has no HuggingFace repository and no file to read. Give its publisher's declaration alone, without --model, --model-file or --target:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project support-bot --version 1.0 \
  --ai-declare support-bot-declaration.json --generate-only

The declaration names the base models (model.baseModels[].ref) and the HuggingFace datasets (datasets[].ref, as huggingface:<owner>/<name>), which are read from the hub by id as in a model scan. Data the hub does not hold goes under datasets[].local. The scan runs in the base image and passes HF_TOKEN when it is set. In the web UI, the Enter model information tile in the AI model group asks the same questions step by step and uses the answers as the declaration. See The SPDX 3.0.1 AI document in the AI model guide.

Deliverables: notice, ML-BOM (CycloneDX 1.7), risk report, G7 conformance, SPDX 3.0.1 AI document

docs.title: When you have the model file, not the model id
docs.text:
A supplier ships weights rather than a Hub link, or the model is internal and was never published. Point at the file itself:

$SBOM --project internal-llm --version 1.0.0 \
  --model-file ./models/internal-llm-q4.gguf \
  --generate-only

Reads the file's own header; no network, no HuggingFace account, and no opt-in image. For the recognized formats, what each one contributes to the SBOM, and the pickle/Keras code-execution check, see Scanning a model file in the AI model guide.

Deliverables are the same as Scenario 7's, minus what the model card would have supplied.

docs.title: Reading the four deliverables
docs.text:
• Notice (NOTICE): components grouped by license. Use it to satisfy the obligation to include or disclose notices when distributing.
  • SBOM: CycloneDX 1.6 by default, or 1.7 with --spec-version 1.7. The artifact you upload to a vulnerability-management system.
  • Open-source risk report: aggregates vulnerabilities by severity with recommended deadlines (Critical 7 days, High 30 days). Includes a license summary and the format conformance result.
  • Conformance check report: the per-item check of whether the SBOM meets the submission quality criteria (required fields, PURL coverage, transitive dependencies, and more). The file is produced by default alongside the other three; the web UI shows it as a screen only on the --analyze path (see above). See Reading the conformance check report in the supplier SBOM guide.

docs.title: All at once in the web UI
docs.text:
If you are not comfortable with the CLI, use the web UI.

$SBOM --ui   # http://localhost:8080 in the browser

Pick a scan target at the top of the UI and provide the matching input.

Scan target Input Current folder scans the source in the folder where the UI was launched Directory path a subfolder under the launch folder (e.g. an OS rootfs), a folder mounted with --ui --mount <dir>, or a folder picked with the desktop app's "Add folder" button GitHub URL enter the URL ZIP upload upload a .zip/tar file Package upload upload a build artifact — .jar, .war, .ear, .deb, .rpm, .whl SBOM upload upload an existing SBOM (JSON), ANALYZE mode Firmware upload upload a .bin, etc. — the tile appears automatically whenever Docker is running Docker image enter the image name AI model enter a HuggingFace model id — the tile appears automatically whenever Docker is running Model file upload a .gguf, .safetensors, .pt, etc. (up to 8 GB) Published dataset enter a Figshare item (its page URL, its DOI, or the item number) or a HuggingFace dataset (datasets/<owner>/<name> or its https://huggingface.co/datasets/... address) in the same field as the model id Enter model information answer the questions about a model that has no repository or file yet (base models, training data, release date and the like)

This table lists what the input scenarios in this guide cover; the full set (12 targets) is in the web UI reference.

For source-code scans (current folder, GitHub URL, ZIP upload), a Result quality group offers toggles (License scan / ScanCode, File-level identification / SCANOSS) that change how the source is analyzed rather than which files are produced, both off by default. See Result quality in the Web UI reference for what each one does and per-target availability.

As it runs, logs stream live; when done you can view or download the notice, SBOM, and risk report. The conformance check report file is downloadable too; its pass/fail screen only appears when the input was an uploaded SBOM (--analyze) rather than a fresh scan.

The firmware upload tab appears automatically whenever the Docker engine is running. See the firmware guide for how it works and how to point it at a different image tag.

docs.title: Troubleshooting / limits
docs.text:
• GitHub URL: for a private repo, the CLI authenticates with the GIT_TOKEN environment variable; the web UI has its own token field below the URL input instead (the two are separate paths). Disallowed URL forms (shell metacharacters, .., spaces) are rejected for security.
  • ZIP/tar: archives containing a path escape (zip-slip) are rejected. If Git Bash on Windows has no unzip, tar is used.
  • C/C++: pure source without a package manager produces a sparse SBOM (see Scenario 3).
  • Firmware: statically linked libraries and vendor-modified squashfs have limited detection (see the firmware analysis guide, Limits).
  • SBOM analysis: converting SPDX to CycloneDX may simplify some license expressions.

Related: Getting started | CLI reference

docs.title: Use in CI/CD
docs.text:
An SBOM is a point-in-time snapshot of dependencies, so it must be regenerated whenever dependencies change to stay in sync with the code. In CI it refreshes on every build and release, attaches to release artifacts, and becomes the basis for a vulnerability policy gate.

Important: a scan reports vulnerabilities and exits successfully unless you ask it to gate. --fail-on makes the scan itself exit non-zero when a condition you name is met (exit 4), or cannot be judged from what the scan produced (exit 5): a finding at a severity or worse, a known malicious package, a license conflict, a scan that found no software (empty-result), or license coverage below a percentage you set (license-coverage=<0-100>). --fail-on-conformance does the same for the conformance check report (exit 2). See Exit codes. No separate step that inspects the report files is needed.

To reduce load, split depth by trigger: on PRs generate the SBOM quickly (--generate-only --no-report); on main and releases generate everything (--all --generate-only) and apply the gate.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
name: SBOM

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  release:
    types: [published]

jobs:
  # PR: lightweight SBOM only (no report)
  sbom-pr:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/sktelecom/bomlens.git /tmp/bomlens
      - run: docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest
      - name: Generate SBOM (lightweight)
        run: |
          /tmp/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh \
            --project "${{ github.event.repository.name }}" \
            --version "${{ github.sha }}" \
            --generate-only --no-report
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: sbom-pr
          path: "*/*_bom.json"

  # main/release: full generation + vulnerability gate
  sbom-full:
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/sktelecom/bomlens.git /tmp/bomlens
      - run: docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest
      - name: Generate SBOM + reports
        run: |
          /tmp/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh \
            --project "${{ github.event.repository.name }}" \
            --version "${{ github.sha }}" \
            --all --generate-only --fail-on-conformance \
            --fail-on vulnerability=critical --fail-on malicious-package

      # The scan above already failed this step if the conformance check report says
      # "fail" (exit 2), if a Critical finding or a malicious package was found
      # (exit 4), or if either could not be judged (exit 5). Add
      # `--license <SPDX id> --fail-on license-conflict` to gate on license
      # conflicts too. Outputs land in a {project}_{version}/ subfolder (see the
      # CLI reference), hence the */ glob below.

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()   # keep reports even when the gate fails
        with:
          name: sbom
          path: |
            */*_bom.json
            */*_security.*
            */*_risk-report.*

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
The scan itself gates, so the job needs no jq.

generate-sbom:
  stage: security
  image: docker:latest
  services:
    - docker:dind
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache git
    - git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/sktelecom/bomlens.git /tmp/bomlens
  script:
    - docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest
    - /tmp/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh
        --project "$CI_PROJECT_NAME"
        --version "$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
        --all --generate-only --fail-on-conformance
        --fail-on vulnerability=critical --fail-on malicious-package
    # The scan already fails this job: exit 2 if the conformance check report says
    # "fail", 4 if a Critical finding or a malicious package was found, 5 if
    # either could not be judged. Outputs land in a {project}_{version}/
    # subfolder (see the CLI reference), hence the */ globs below.
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - "*/*_bom.json"
      - "*/*_security.*"

docs.title: Declared components in CI
docs.text:
Your own executables, libraries and firmware, and the vendor binaries or copied sources a scan cannot find, are listed in a declaration file kept in the repository (see Declaring your own components). The scan reads the build outputs that file names, so the job builds first and scans after. This release job also checks the result against BSI TR-03183-2 and takes the version from the tag.

name: Release SBOM

on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  sbom:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build
        run: make   # writes the files sbom-declared.cdx.json names, e.g. out/bin/media-daemon
      - run: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/sktelecom/bomlens.git /tmp/bomlens
      - run: docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          /tmp/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh \
            --project "${{ github.event.repository.name }}" \
            --version "${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}" \
            --components sbom-declared.cdx.json \
            --conformance-profile bsi-tr-03183-2 --fail-on-conformance \
            --supplier "Example Corp <https://example.com>" \
            --sbom-author "Example Corp <sbom@example.com>" \
            --license Apache-2.0 \
            --generate-only

      # A declaration file that is refused (a build output it names is missing,
      # a component has no bomlens:origin, and so on) fails this step with exit
      # 1. The SBOM is then kept as {project}_{version}_bom.refused.json, not
      # _bom.json, so nothing downstream takes the incomplete one. A BSI row
      # that fails ends the step with exit 2 (--fail-on-conformance).

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()   # keep the conformance report and a refused SBOM too
        with:
          name: sbom
          path: |
            */*_bom.json
            */*_conformance.*
            */*_bom.refused.json

${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v} turns the tag v2.1.0 into 2.1.0, which a first-party component without its own version takes. --components names the file explicitly; without it, sbom-declared.cdx.json at the repository root is read anyway. --license takes an SPDX identifier.

docs.title: When the runner has no Docker
docs.text:
scan-sbom.sh starts containers, so it needs a Docker engine: a runner without one (a Kubernetes runner, a GitLab job without docker:dind) cannot use the examples above. Run the scanner image itself as the job image instead. A source scan inside it needs no Docker socket when a lock file covers the whole tree (a package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, bun.lock or gradle.lockfile, with no other manifest below the root): it reads the lock file as it is and fills the licenses it lacks from the package registry. A tree without such a lock file is read by syft from its manifests, which gives direct dependencies only (a Node project with none is refused with guidance), so commit a lock file or use a runner that has Docker.

generate-sbom:
  stage: security
  image:
    name: ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    MODE: SOURCE
    SOURCE_ROOT: $CI_PROJECT_DIR
    PROJECT_NAME: $CI_PROJECT_NAME
    PROJECT_VERSION: $CI_COMMIT_SHA
    GENERATE_NOTICE: "true"
    GENERATE_SECURITY: "true"
    UPLOAD_ENABLED: "false"
    HOST_OUTPUT_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/sbom-out
    FAIL_ON: "vulnerability=critical,malicious-package"
  script:
    - mkdir -p sbom-out && cd sbom-out
    - /usr/local/bin/run-scan
    # In a direct run the gate's verdict is a file, not an exit code: fail the job
    # when a condition was met (status "met") or could not be judged ("unjudged").
    - '! grep -qE "^(met|unjudged)" *_gate.result'
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - sbom-out/

The variables are the ones of the direct docker run; the scan reads the project from SOURCE_ROOT and writes into the folder it runs in.

Related: CLI reference | Generate notice, security & risk reports | What the reports mean

docs.title: Declaring your own components
docs.text:
A source scan reads package managers and lock files, so it finds the open source a project depends on. It cannot find what you built yourself, or what was put into the tree by hand. A declaration file lists those components. A source scan adds them to the SBOM and reads the hashes and file properties from the build outputs you name, so nobody has to type them in.

This is what the bsi-tr-03183-2 conformance profile measures, and what lets your own components pass a submission review without a purl. Both are covered at the end of this page.

docs.title: What goes in the file?
docs.text:
Only what the scan cannot find. Typically:

  • your own executables, libraries, firmware images and archives, one component per delivered program or file
  • binaries a vendor supplied, such as a chip vendor's driver or a prebuilt library
  • source copied into the tree without a package manager, such as a HAL or an RTOS

Open source that a package manager or lock file brings in is found by the scan and does not belong in the file. Scan once without a declaration file and list only what is missing from that SBOM. A component listed in both places is kept twice (the scan warns when the two have the same purl). For open source copied into C/C++ source, --identify-vendored can identify part of it from the files themselves.

docs.title: Where does the file go?
docs.text:
A source scan reads sbom-declared.cdx.json at the root of the scan target when that file exists. To keep the file elsewhere, or to split it, pass --components <file>; repeat the option for several files, for example one per module in a monorepo or one per vendor directory. With --components, the file at the root is not read.

Whichever file a component is written in, a bomlens:artifact path is relative to the scan target root, not to the declaration file.

--no-components skips the file at the root, for a scan made before the build outputs it names exist. It cannot be combined with --components.

Declaration files are read by source scans and by a Yocto build directory given as --target (see A Yocto image); a firmware, image, binary or --analyze run stops with an error when given --components. The web UI has no --components option: put sbom-declared.cdx.json at the root of the folder you scan, a source tree or a Yocto build directory. Its Read sbom-declared.cdx.json switch under Result quality, on by default, is the UI's --no-components. When the file is refused, the failed scan lists the reasons and offers the _bom.refused.json to view or download, and in a finished scan the Components section marks each declared component with a "first-party" or "third-party" badge. See the web UI reference.

docs.title: What does the file look like?
docs.text:
The file is a CycloneDX document that holds only components (and, if you want, dependencies). Field names are the standard CycloneDX ones.

{
  "bomFormat": "CycloneDX",
  "specVersion": "1.6",
  "components": [
    {
      "type": "application",
      "name": "media-daemon",
      "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
      "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
      "properties": [
        { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
        { "name": "bomlens:artifact", "value": "out/bin/media-daemon" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "library",
      "name": "vendor-hal",
      "version": "4.2.0",
      "supplier": { "name": "Example Chip Vendor", "url": ["https://chip.example.com"] },
      "licenses": [ { "license": { "id": "BSD-3-Clause" } } ],
      "properties": [
        { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "third-party" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

bomFormat must be CycloneDX and components must be an array; specVersion is optional.

Every component needs the property bomlens:origin, given once, with the value first-party (built by you) or third-party (received from someone else). There is no default value. With a default, a vendor binary left unmarked could count as your own and skip the purl requirement described below.

A first-party component without a version takes the product version (--version). A third-party component must give the version it was received at.

bomlens:artifact names a build output, as a path relative to the scan target root with forward slashes. It is optional, and may repeat when a component is delivered as several files. Leave it out for a component that has no file of its own, such as a HAL or RTOS compiled into the firmware.

bomlens:distribution-url is optional: where the delivered file can be downloaded, as an http or https URL or a relative path inside the delivery. Without it, the build output's path is used.

dependencies is optional. Each ref must be a component of the same file, and dependsOn may name a component of any declaration file or one the scan found, by bom-ref. A component without a bom-ref gets declared:<name>@<version>.

docs.title: Which CycloneDX fields can a component use?
docs.text: name, version, bom-ref, group, description, copyright, cpe, purl, publisher, author, mime-type, type, scope, tags, supplier, manufacturer, authors, hashes, licenses, externalReferences and properties. Each is checked against the shape the CycloneDX 1.6 schema gives it. Any other field, nested components included, is refused by name rather than copied into the SBOM unchecked. List every component at the top level of the file.

docs.title: How are licences written?
docs.text:
A licence id must be on the SPDX License List. For a licence the list does not hold, such as your own proprietary terms, use name with a LicenseRef- value made of letters, digits, . and -, for example LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary. A plain name such as Proprietary is accepted by the scan, but the BSI profile reads only an SPDX id, an expression or a LicenseRef- name. One SPDX expression can be given instead of a list.

A licence given without an acknowledgement is written as concluded, the licence the component is distributed under, which is the distribution licence BSI TR-03183-2 asks for. An acknowledgement the file gives is kept.

docs.title: What does BomLens fill in?
docs.text:
For a component with one build output, read from the file itself:

  • the SHA-512 and SHA-256 hashes
  • bsi:component:filename, the file name without its path
  • bsi:component:executable (executable for an ELF program or shared library, a PE file or a Mach-O binary), bsi:component:archive (archive for zip, tar, gzip, bzip2, xz, zstd, lz4, 7z, rar, ar and deb, rpm, cpio and ISO 9660) and bsi:component:structured (structured for an archive that lists its contents, a compressed tar included; a plain program, a firmware image and a single compressed stream are unstructured)
  • an externalReferences entry of type distribution carrying the SHA-512, with bomlens:distribution-url or the build output's path as its url

A value the file gives for one of the three bsi:component:* properties is kept instead of the one read from the build output. A hash the file gives must match the build output.

A component with several build outputs gets one nested component of type file per output, each with its own hashes, properties and distribution entry, and carries no hashes itself, since one set of hashes cannot describe several files.

The product depends on each declared component (in a file with dependencies, on each one nothing else depends on), so the dependency graph reaches all of them. Every component added this way carries bomlens:declared true.

docs.title: What is refused, and why?
docs.text:
A file that breaks a rule is refused. The scan prints every reason with the file and component, stops before the SBOM is normalized, signed or uploaded, and exits 1. The SBOM written up to that point is kept as {Project}_{Version}_bom.refused.json, not _bom.json, so a later step that picks up _bom.json cannot take the incomplete one. The next scan of the same project and version removes it.

Refused Why bomlens:origin missing, given twice, or not first-party or third-party without it a vendor's binary could pass as your own and skip the purl requirement a third-party component without version the version received is what vulnerabilities are matched against, and the scan cannot guess it a bomlens:artifact file that does not exist a file that silently drops out is the same omission as writing the list by hand. When the file at the scan root was read by default, the message points to --no-components; a file under an --exclude path is reported as excluded a bomlens:artifact path that is absolute, contains .. or a backslash, leads out through a symbolic link, or is not a regular file the build output has to be inside what was scanned the same name and version in two places, in one file or across files one component, one entry a bom-ref already used by a component the scan found, or used twice references must point to one component a field outside the list above, nested components, or a value of the wrong shape the file is outside input, and nothing goes into the SBOM unchecked a licence id not on the SPDX License List use a LicenseRef- name instead (the message suggests one) a hash that does not match the build output, a BLAKE3 hash, or hashes on a component with several build outputs a hash that cannot be checked against the file is not trusted a bsi:component:* value other than the ones BSI TR-03183-2 defines, or one given for a component with several build outputs each value describes one file a bomlens:distribution-url that is neither an http(s) URL nor a relative path inside the delivery, or one given for a component with several build outputs each build output is named by its own path a dependencies entry naming a component that is neither declared nor found by the scan the graph must stay connected a file over 4 MiB, with more than 10,000 components, not UTF-8 JSON, or not a CycloneDX document the file has to be a CycloneDX document of a size the scan can check

docs.title: When does a first-party component need no purl?
docs.text:
Your own build outputs are not published to a package repository, so they have no purl. In every conformance profile, skt-submission included, a declared component is left out of the PURL coverage, "Traceable PURL (no pkg:generic)" and "No upstream purl" rows when all of these hold:

  • its bomlens:origin is first-party
  • it has a supplier with a name or URL
  • it has a SHA-512, which BomLens computes from its bomlens:artifact file (or every one of its nested files has one)
  • it was added by the declaration file in this same scan

Such components are listed by name on the advisory row "First-party components identified by supplier and SHA-512 instead of a purl". A third-party component still needs a purl, and nothing is exempted when an SBOM is checked with --analyze, even one that marks components first-party. See Reading the conformance check report.

docs.title: Checking the SBOM against BSI TR-03183-2
docs.text:
./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project MediaBox --version 2.1.0 \
  --conformance-profile bsi-tr-03183-2 --fail-on-conformance \
  --supplier "Example Corp <https://example.com>" \
  --sbom-author "Example Corp <sbom@example.com>" \
  --license LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary

The profile measures BSI TR-03183-2 v2.1.0. It requires CycloneDX 1.6 or later (the default output), and:

  • an SBOM creator with an email address or URL: --sbom-author "Name <email>" writes it to metadata.authors
  • the product (metadata.component) with a creator that has a URL or email (--supplier "Name <https://...>" or "Name <email>"), a name, a version (--version), and a concluded licence (--license, an SPDX identifier, expression or LicenseRef- name, written as concluded)
  • a dependency graph that reaches every component from the product. The row warns when the SBOM does not state its completeness (compositions)
  • for each declared component, a supplier or manufacturer with a URL or contact email, a name and version, and a concluded licence as an SPDX identifier, expression or LicenseRef- name
  • for each declared component that names a build output, its file name, SHA-512 and the three file properties, which BomLens fills from bomlens:artifact

A declared library or framework with no file of its own (linked into another component) is listed on an advisory row instead of failing the file rows. A declared component of any other type without a file, an application or firmware for example, fails them. The components the scan found are measured on one advisory row, with counts and each component's gaps, and do not change the result. PURL coverage is advisory in this profile.

A row that fails makes the report say "fail"; --fail-on-conformance turns that into exit code 2. The full rule list is in the CLI reference under --conformance-profile.

docs.title: Examples by platform
docs.text: The examples show only the components entries; put them in a file shaped like the one above.

docs.title: A Linux application in C/C++
docs.text:
A C/C++ application with a Conan lock file: the scan reads conan.lock for the open source, and the declaration file lists the programs the build writes to out/bin/.

{
  "type": "application",
  "name": "media-daemon",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:artifact", "value": "out/bin/media-daemon" }
  ]
}

Run the build before the scan, so out/bin/media-daemon exists when it is read.

docs.title: An Android device build
docs.text:
Scan the tree that holds out/. Vendor binaries that come prebuilt are third-party with the version the vendor gave; a service you build yourself is first-party.

{
  "type": "library",
  "name": "libvendor-camera",
  "version": "3.4.1",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Chip Vendor", "url": ["https://chip.example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleChipVendor-Binary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "third-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:artifact", "value": "out/target/product/<device>/vendor/lib64/libvendor-camera.so" }
  ]
},
{
  "type": "application",
  "name": "example-camera-service",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:artifact", "value": "out/target/product/<device>/vendor/bin/hw/example-camera-service" }
  ]
}

Replace <device> with the product name of the build. When the vendor directories have different owners, keep one declaration file per directory and pass each with --components.

docs.title: A Zephyr application
docs.text:
The build writes the firmware to build/zephyr/zephyr.elf. The scan does not read west.yml, so the Zephyr kernel and the modules it pins are listed by hand, with the revision west.yml pins as the version. They are compiled into the firmware, so they have no file of their own.

{
  "type": "firmware",
  "name": "sensor-node-fw",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:artifact", "value": "build/zephyr/zephyr.elf" }
  ]
},
{
  "type": "library",
  "name": "zephyr",
  "version": "4.1.0",
  "supplier": { "name": "Zephyr Project", "url": ["https://www.zephyrproject.org"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "id": "Apache-2.0" } } ],
  "properties": [ { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "third-party" } ]
}

Add one third-party entry like the second for each module in west.yml that ends up in the firmware, such as a vendor HAL.

docs.title: Bare-metal firmware with a vendored HAL and RTOS
docs.text:
The vendor HAL and the RTOS are copied into the tree and compiled into build/firmware.bin. The firmware names its file; the HAL and the RTOS are third-party libraries without bomlens:artifact.

{
  "type": "firmware",
  "name": "motor-controller-fw",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:artifact", "value": "build/firmware.bin" }
  ]
},
{
  "type": "library",
  "name": "freertos-kernel",
  "version": "11.1.0",
  "supplier": { "name": "FreeRTOS", "url": ["https://www.freertos.org"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "id": "MIT" } } ],
  "properties": [ { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "third-party" } ]
},
{
  "type": "library",
  "name": "example-mcu-hal",
  "version": "1.8.0",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Chip Vendor", "url": ["https://chip.example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "id": "BSD-3-Clause" } } ],
  "properties": [ { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "third-party" } ]
}

Under the BSI profile the two libraries appear on the advisory row for declared libraries with no file of their own.

docs.title: A Yocto image
docs.text:
A Yocto build records its packages in its own SPDX output, which BomLens reads from the build directory (see Yocto images in the supplier SBOM guide). The packages are already there, with their versions, purls and file hashes, so a declaration names the recipe (PN) in bomlens:yocto-recipe instead of a build output, and adds what the build does not know: the supplier, the concluded licence and the origin.

{
  "type": "application",
  "name": "media-daemon",
