  "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:yocto-recipe", "value": "media-daemon" }
  ]
},
{
  "type": "firmware",
  "name": "vendor-dsp",
  "supplier": { "name": "Example Chip Vendor", "url": ["https://chip.example.com"] },
  "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-Vendor-Binary" } } ],
  "properties": [
    { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "third-party" },
    { "name": "bomlens:yocto-recipe", "value": "vendor-dsp" }
  ]
}

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project MediaBox --version 2.1.0 \
  --target build --components sbom-declared.cdx.json \
  --conformance-profile bsi-tr-03183-2

Every package the image installs from that recipe, such as media-daemon and media-daemon-cli, gets the declared type, supplier, licence and origin, and keeps its own name, version, purl and CPE. The files the build recorded for each package are nested under it with their hashes (SHA-512 from Yocto 6.1). A version may be left out; one that differs from the build's is refused. On the command line a Yocto build directory has no default file, so --components is always given. The web UI, which cannot name a file, reads sbom-declared.cdx.json at the root of the build directory picked with the Directory input. A multilib or SDK variant such as lib32-media-daemon is a recipe of its own and is declared separately. A recipe the image did not install, or a component added by name with the name of an installed package, is refused.

docs.title: Using it in CI
docs.text:
The declaration file belongs in the repository, next to the build that produces the files it names. A CI job builds first, then scans; see Declared components in CI for a GitHub Actions example.

Related: CLI reference | Artifacts | Use in CI/CD | Supplier SBOM validation

docs.title: Firmware analysis guide
docs.text: How to identify components and check the SBOM, licenses, and vulnerabilities in a network-device firmware binary (.bin, .img, squashfs, and so on). Use it when you only have the binary and no source, such as firmware received from a supplier.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Firmware is a single file that packs and seals an operating system and dozens of libraries. Feeding a firmware file straight into a normal scan detects almost nothing and yields an empty SBOM. Firmware analysis first unpacks the contents, then identifies components.

  1. Unpack the firmware (unblob, falling back to unsquashfs, 7z, then binwalk) to extract the rootfs.
  2. Use syft to identify components installed by a package manager (opkg, dpkg, apk, rpm). An image can carry more than one filesystem, and a tree sitting beside the rootfs rather than inside it is cataloged too. Three kinds are recognized, each by the record of what is installed in it rather than by its directory name: a container image store, identified by the image index Docker keeps (the usual layout on a switch OS, where most of what runs is in a container); a second filesystem carrying its own package database; and an interpreter's installed library set, such as a Python site-packages. Set FW_EXTRA_ROOTS=false to read only the rootfs. Components from a container store record the image they belong to in bomlens:container:image, and the images themselves appear as container components. A package installed by dpkg inside a container is identified by the distribution the container runs, read from the os-release in its own layers, so that the vulnerability step has something to match it against; those carry bomlens:purlSource. An SPDX export keeps this: the images and the distribution are packages there, and the membership is a CONTAINS relationship.
  3. Use the signature checkers of cve-bin-tool to identify stripped static binaries (busybox, openssl, dropbear, and so on) and give them a CPE.
  4. Merge the two results into one SBOM, then run the same post-processing as a normal scan (licenses, CVEs, signing). CVEs of components with no package PURL come from the NVD CPE index in the image (see How CVEs are matched).

docs.title: Preparing the firmware image
docs.text:
Firmware analysis needs a separate image that bundles the unpacking and binary-identification tools (unblob, cve-bin-tool, and so on). These are GPL-family tools, so they are kept out of the lightweight base image and split into an opt-in firmware image.

docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-firmware:latest

This image is the default, so adding --firmware pulls it without any extra setting. To use a different tag, set the environment variable SBOM_FIRMWARE_IMAGE.

In the web UI and the desktop app you do not have to run that command: the firmware input offers a Download now button with the download size, and shows how many layers are done while it runs. Without it the image is still pulled on the first firmware scan, so the only difference is whether the wait happens before the scan or inside it.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text: Firmware analysis needs the firmware image (above), whether you use the web UI or the CLI.

docs.title: From the web UI
docs.text:
Launch the web UI as usual — you do not need to point it at this image yourself. As long as the Docker engine is running, the base UI image launches this firmware image as a sibling container over the Docker socket, and the firmware upload tile appears automatically.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --ui
#   Windows: just double-click sbom-ui.bat

Set SBOM_FIRMWARE_IMAGE only if you want a different tag or an internal mirror registry. It takes effect only as a real environment variable — the settings file bomlens.settings.txt that a double-clicked .bat reads does not support this key.

SBOM_FIRMWARE_IMAGE=<your-mirror>:<tag> ./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --ui

Enter a project name and version, choose the firmware upload tile, upload the file, and run.

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
Pass the firmware file you received to --target and add --firmware:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project device-fw --version 1.0.0 \
  --target "./device.bin" --firmware \
  --all --generate-only
  • Recognized extensions (.bin, .img, .squashfs, .sqsh, .ubi, .ubifs, .trx, .chk, .fw, .rom, .dlf, .bix) are auto-detected even without --firmware, but being explicit is recommended.
  • The outputs are the same three as a normal scan: the notice (_NOTICE), the SBOM (_bom.json), and the risk report (_risk-report).
  • A release folder can be passed as it is. When --target is a folder with no manifest or build file at its top level that directly holds one firmware image or one extracted root filesystem (for example images/ with rootfs/, install/, a kernel and an image file), that image or root filesystem is scanned and the scan prints which one. A file counts as a firmware image by its firmware or filesystem signature, or by an extension used for firmware (.bix, .trx, .chk, .dlf, .ubi, .ubifs, .squashfs, .sqsh, .rom, .fw, .jffs2, .cramfs); a .bin or .img needs the signature. A folder with executables, shared libraries, .asar, node_modules, model weights or tokenizer files at its top level, or with more than 20 top-level files, is scanned as source, so an unpacked desktop app, a model snapshot or a build output staging folder keeps its source scan. When there are several, the scan stops and lists the --target for each. When the root filesystem it picked has no package database and the firmware image is not present, the warning also lists the larger files beside it (over 1 MiB, at most five) as --target "<file>" --firmware commands to try. --as-source scans the folder itself as source instead.
  • A root filesystem folder from the build can be passed instead of the firmware file. When the folder has no package database (apk, dpkg or rpm) and the firmware image is present, its binaries are identified the same way as after unpacking a firmware file, and the result and the version template are the same. Without the firmware image the scan reads the folder as a root filesystem and says which image to pull. --firmware with a folder does the same for any folder holding an unpacked image. The folder is copied for the scan and mounted read-only, so nothing in it is changed. A Yocto build directory is refused with --firmware, since the scan reads what the build recorded.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The output is the same NOTICE, SBOM and risk report as any other scan (see What the reports mean and the artifacts reference for the general shape), but a firmware SBOM has one thing worth knowing before you read it: some components carry no version at all. When a binary's version string did not survive the build, BomLens still records that the library is linked in — read from the ELF's SONAME and NEEDED entries, structure rather than a string match — and tags that component bomlens:evidenceGrade = presence-only. A missing version there is not a gap in the scan; it means the binary itself carries no version to read, and the component is real regardless. For a license obligation this is enough (the library is present whether or not anything says which release), but it means version-based CVE matching has nothing to key on for that component.

The unpacker also reports how much of the image it could open, and BomLens records that beside the result. The totals go on the firmware component as bomlens:firmware:* properties (input-bytes, recognized-regions, unknown-regions, unknown-bytes, unknown-top-level-percent, nested-unknown-regions, encrypted-regions, extraction-failed, extraction-failed-formats, missing-extractors), and the risk report adds a "Firmware analysis scope" section when any part of the image went unopened. Read it as the scope of the scan: components inside a region that was not recognized, was encrypted, or needed an extraction tool the scanner image does not include are not in the SBOM, so a clean vulnerability table describes only what could be opened. The unrecognized share and byte count are measured at the top level of the image; unrecognized regions inside extracted content are counted apart. The section is written only for a scan BomLens ran itself, not for an SBOM you submit for review. Only totals are kept; the unpacker's full report is not written to the output folder.

If the syft package-identification pass fails, the scan does not stop: syft's own error goes into the scan log, and the SBOM records which pass failed as bomlens:pipeline-step-failed (firmware-packages for the main rootfs; firmware-extra-roots for a secondary package source unpacking finds alongside it, such as a nested container image store or a filesystem with its own package database). A component count lower than expected is worth checking the scan log for this before assuming the firmware genuinely holds that few packages.

docs.title: Upstream repository purl
docs.text:
A component read out of a binary or a firmware package database has no purl, a pkg:generic one, or a pkg:opkg one. None of these names a project, so a tool that looks components up by purl cannot identify it even when the name and version are right. A component read from a Yocto build's own records has the same gap. For firmware, root filesystem and binary scans, and for an SBOM read from a Yocto build's records (a Yocto build directory as --target, or its SPDX or manifests under --analyze), BomLens sets the purl of the project's upstream source repository at its release tag, for example pkg:github/mirror/busybox@1_22_1, pkg:github/gregkh/linux@v3.10.18, pkg:sourceforge/boa@0.94.13 or pkg:gnu/readline@5.2.

The conversion uses a closed table (docker/lib/upstream-purl-map.json) of projects whose repository and tag spelling were checked: BusyBox, curl, OpenSSL 1.x and 3.x, OpenSSH, Linux, zlib, U-Boot, Net-SNMP, ncurses, net-tools, libxml2, SQLite, glibc, Dropbear, Mbed TLS, Python, Boa, readline, jansson, json-c, libbpf, iproute2, musl and util-linux. json-c tags carry a release date, so only the listed versions 0.13.1 to 0.19 are covered. A component is matched by its own name, by the name of what it was built from, or by its CPE. The name it was built from is the Yocto recipe (bomlens:yocto:recipe, so openssl-bin and libssl3 are read as openssl), the OpenWrt source package (the last part of syft:metadata:source, so libmbedtls12 is read as mbedtls and ip-full as iproute2), or the product of a CPE whose vendor is *, the form in which Yocto writes CVE_PRODUCT. A toolchain package (an OpenWrt source path ending in toolchain, such as libc) and a kernel module package (kmod-*, built from package/kernel/linux) are not read by their source package name, so they keep what they had; a kmod-* package does not take the kernel's purl. A match is used only when it has a version of a form the table covers; a package rebuild count such as -1 and a kernel build hash are removed first, and a Linux or glibc base release written 5.4.0 takes the tag of 5.4. A component not in the table keeps the identifier it had, since a guessed repository or tag would name a different version. The one exception is a source download address that states the release, for a project the table does not list (for a listed project the table decides). The Yocto SPDX 2.2 reader records the address of the recipe's first source as bomlens:sourceUrl; a GitHub release asset or tag archive there gives pkg:github/<owner>/<repo>@<tag> when the tag names the component's version (v1.2, V_1_2, name-1.2 or 1.2), and a GNU release (ftp.gnu.org or ftpmirror.gnu.org, /gnu/<name>/<name>-<version>.tar.*) gives pkg:gnu/<name>@<version> when that version equals the component's. A plain tarball elsewhere or a git commit is not read as a release. When a scan reports a project both as the operating-system component and as a package or binary with the same purl, as syft does for BusyBox, only the package or binary gets the purl. The version, the CPE and the evidence are not changed, so the CVEs found from them stay in the report. The new purl is marked bomlens:purlSource = upstream-map, and a purl it replaced is kept in bomlens:originalPurl. Set ENRICH_UPSTREAM_PURL=false to turn it off.

docs.title: Supplying the versions the scan could not read
docs.text:
A component tagged presence-only has no version, so neither a CVE lookup nor a purl lookup can use it. Every firmware, root filesystem and binary scan lists those components on the console and writes them to <Project>_<Version>_component-versions.template.csv. Write the version shipped in the product after each name and pass the file back:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project device-fw --version 1.0.0 \
  --target "./device.bin" --firmware \
  --component-versions device-fw_1.0.0_component-versions.template.csv --generate-only

The file is CSV with the columns name,version,reason; the third column is optional, so a two-column name,version file is read as before. Lines starting with # and rows with neither a version nor a reason are skipped. The template can be filled in where it is: when the file passed is that template, the scan leaves it as you wrote it and only lists what is still missing. A filled version is marked bomlens:versionSource = supplier-declared and gets the upstream purl above. When the scan read a version from the delivered files, that version is kept and a warning shows both, because a source tree can hold several releases of one project and the binary shows which one shipped. A name the scan did not find is added as a component marked bomlens:identifiedBy = supplier-declared. A file over 256 KiB, a row that is not two or three fields, a name or version with characters outside letters, digits and . _ + ~ -, or one name given two versions is refused with the line number: the SBOM and the other files are written without the file's versions, and the scan exits 1. A component whose version reads UNKNOWN (a kernel module with no version in its metadata) counts as having none, so it is in the template. A component whose name holds other characters, such as a space, is listed on the console instead of in the template.

When a component has no version to give, leave the version empty and write a reason instead. The reason is one of own-code (the manufacturer's own code), not-open-source (only the name matches an open source project) or version-unknown (open source, but the shipped version cannot be confirmed); case is ignored, and any other value, or one name given two different reasons, refuses the file with the line number. The component stays in the SBOM without a version and carries bomlens:versionReason with the reason. A row with both a version and a reason applies the version and ignores the reason with a warning, and a reason given for a component the scan read a version for, or for a name the scan did not find, is ignored with a warning. A version-unknown component is still listed in the security report under the components that could not be checked.

name,version,reason
busybox,1.36.1,
libvendor,,own-code
telnetd,,not-open-source
libfoo,,version-unknown

The template has the header name,version,reason and comment lines that explain the three reasons, and it leaves out components that already carry a reason.

docs.title: How CVEs are matched
docs.text:
Trivy matches components by their package PURL, with a database it downloads at scan time as in any other scan. A component with no package PURL (none, pkg:generic, pkg:opkg, or a source repository PURL such as pkg:github) is matched by its CPE against the NVD CPE index built into the image (cpe_match.sqlite), and its CVEs go into the same security report. This match runs with --security in firmware, root filesystem and binary scans and for a Yocto SPDX 2.2 archive (<image>.spdx.tar.zst), once, after every step that adds CPEs. A component identified by name and version through BomLens's name list (cpe-name-map.json), OpenSSH or BusyBox for example, is matched as well as one the signature checkers gave a CPE. A Yocto SPDX 3.0 document and a build read through its manifests are not matched this way: they already carry Yocto's own verdicts, and matching their CPEs again would report as open what Yocto judged patched or not affected. Yocto writes a CPE such as cpe:2.3:*:*:busybox:1.36.1. A part of * is read as an application, and a vendor of * is looked up by product alone across every vendor of that product, as Yocto's own cve-check does. Most products listed under more than one vendor are one project that NVD filed under several names (linux_kernel under linux and kernel, curl under haxx, curl and daniel_stenberg). Yocto drops the wrong vendors' CVEs with CVE_STATUS cpe-incorrect, which an SPDX 2.2 build does not carry, so a product name another project shares can bring that project's CVEs too. An SPDX 2.2 build does not record which CVEs a recipe patched either, so the CVEs matched this way can include ones the recipe already patched; SPDX 3.0 records it (INHERIT += "create-spdx-3.0"). The result manifest records the step as match-cpe with offered, components and cves counts.

The index is distilled from the NVD data when the image is built, so the match needs no network and no NVD API key, and its data is as recent as the image. Pull a newer image to update it. cve-bin-tool only identifies binaries; it does not download or read a vulnerability database. CVE_BIN_TOOL_MODE=components-only turns the CPE match off while identification still runs. An image built with --build-arg SBOM_CPE_INDEX=false has no index, and the step is recorded as skipped (not_installed).

A component with no version, or with no package PURL and no CPE the index was asked about, is listed in the security report under "Components that could not be checked" (UncheckedComponents in _security.json). A short vulnerability table therefore covers only the components that were checked.

The scan prints "This product uses NVD data but is not endorsed or certified by the NVD.", and the image carries the data attribution in /opt/cve-bin-tool-home/CVE-DATA-NOTICE.txt. OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities) advisories are not bundled, to keep share-alike data out of the redistributed image.

docs.title: License note
docs.text: The firmware image contains GPL tools (cve-bin-tool, sasquatch, and some extractors that unblob depends on). The shell scripts only invoke them as separate processes, so copyleft does not propagate into our code, but redistributing GPL binaries in an image carries the obligation to include the license texts and offer the source. For the full inventory, see Bundled tool licenses. The GPL analysis tools live only in this firmware image. Every image including the base one is Debian-based, though, so all of them also carry GPL system packages; source directions for those are in the same document.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The open-source tool stack detects roughly 60–85% of components, and the result depends heavily on the firmware type, how aggressively it is stripped, and whether unpacking succeeds.
  • Without function-level binary fingerprinting, stripped or inlined components and binaries with version strings removed are missed.
  • Statically linked libraries, vendor-modified squashfs, encrypted or signed firmware, and renamed libraries go undetected or are misidentified.
  • The resulting SBOM is a best-effort estimate, so do not use it as the sole basis for legal license compliance.

Related: Getting started | Scenarios guide | CLI reference | Notice and security guide

docs.title: Identify bundled open source (C/C++)
docs.text: Use this when you scan a C/C++ embedded source tree and BomLens finds almost nothing.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text:
A normal scan reads a package manager (npm, Maven, pip, Go, Conan, and so on) to learn what open source a project uses. C/C++ embedded firmware usually has no package manager: the open source is copied straight into the source tree (this is called vendored source — for example a copy of openssl, zlib, or liblfds under third_party/). cdxgen cannot name those files, so the SBOM comes back almost empty, with each file listed as an unidentified pkg:generic entry.

When that happens, BomLens prints a one-line hint suggesting this option, and the web UI shows the same hint after the scan. You do not need to recognize the situation yourself.

--identify-vendored matches the file fingerprints of your sources against the public OSSKB knowledge base and records each match as a real component (name, version, PURL), so the copied-in open source shows up in the SBOM — and, where the library has known CVEs, in the security report.

docs.title: What is sent
docs.text: Only file fingerprints (hashes) are sent to the OSSKB service. Your source code never leaves the machine. The supplier can run this in their own environment before any contract.

docs.title: On a package-managed project
docs.text:
This option is for source with no package manager. If your project uses npm, Maven, pip, Go, and so on, the normal scan already resolves your dependencies and you do not need it. If you turn it on anyway, BomLens reconciles the results: dependency and build directories (node_modules, vendor, dist, and the like) are skipped, and any match whose name a package-manager component already carries is dropped in favor of that authoritative identity. So enabling it on a managed project does not duplicate known dependencies or inflate the vulnerability count — at most it adds genuinely copied-in source the package manager could not see.

Matches are recorded read-only, tagged with their source and confidence. BomLens does not provide an accept/reject audit workflow; if you need to confirm or triage matches, upload the SBOM to a vulnerability management system (Dependency-Track, TRUSCA, etc.) and do it there.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The published bomlens image already includes the SCANOSS client, so no extra setup is needed. If you build the image yourself with a minimal configuration, add the build arg:

docker build --build-arg SBOM_SCANOSS=true -t bomlens ./docker

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project trelay --version 26.4.0 --target ./src \
  --identify-vendored --all --generate-only

In the web UI or desktop app, open Advanced and turn on File-level identification (SCANOSS) — the on-screen label differs from this guide's title, but it is the same feature. The option appears only for a source scan (current directory, git URL, or ZIP upload) when the image supports it.

If you are on Windows and new to the command line, follow the desktop-app steps in Quick start without the CLI first.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Copied-in open source appears in the SBOM as named components with versions, each tagged vendored (a bomlens:layer=vendored property).
  • Components that map to a known product get a CPE, so the Trivy security report lists their CVEs. For example a vendored openssl 1.1.1w shows up with its advisories.
  • Niche libraries with no entry in the vulnerability databases (for example liblfds, libaes, djbdns) are still identified by name and version; they simply have no CVEs to report, which is a limit of the public data, not of the scan.

Only full-file matches become components. Partial (snippet) matches are noisy and are left out, so the report stays clean.

docs.title: Endpoint and limits
docs.text:
The default endpoint is the free OSSKB API, which is rate-limited and intended for identification only. From the CLI, you can point at a SCANOSS commercial or self-hosted endpoint with environment variables for high-volume or air-gapped use:

SCANOSS_API_URL=https://your-scanoss-endpoint \
SCANOSS_API_KEY=your-key \
./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project trelay --version 26.4.0 --target ./src --identify-vendored --all --generate-only

In the web UI and desktop app, you can supply only the token from the screen. If you hit the free OSSKB rate limit, turn on File-level identification (SCANOSS) and paste a token from scanoss.com into the field that appears below the toggle, then run again. The token is used once for that scan and is never stored or logged.

The endpoint URL (SCANOSS_API_URL) and the reporting threshold (SCANOSS_MIN_FILES) are set through CLI or container environment variables only; neither the web UI nor the desktop app exposes a field for them. In particular, the desktop app does not forward SCANOSS_API_URL into the container, so a commercial or self-hosted endpoint cannot be used from the desktop app today. If you need one, run from the CLI or sbom-ui.bat with the variable set.

Version precision is approximate. A file match reports the release where that file content first appeared, so different files of the same library can resolve to slightly different versions and a copied-in library may be reported a point release off. Treat the version (and any CVEs derived from it) as a starting point for review, not a final verdict.

Attribution can also point at the wrong project. A file that many projects copy (for example zlib's deflate.c) may match a downstream project that vendored it rather than the canonical upstream. To cut that noise, BomLens reports a library only when at least two files agree on it (configurable with SCANOSS_MIN_FILES; set 1 to keep every match) and resolves the version and PURL from the consensus across those files, so scattered one-off fork matches are dropped and a library split across forks collapses to a single component. This helps but does not fully fix it — a real copy can still be reported under another name, and its CVEs missed. It is a ranking and coverage limit of the knowledge base, more pronounced on the free OSSKB; for higher-fidelity attribution, point SCANOSS_API_URL at a SCANOSS commercial or self-hosted endpoint.

Separately, scanning source that is itself published in a public repository will match that repository (your own first-party files can match your own public project) — this does not occur for the intended case of private supplier source.

Results are a best-effort estimate that benefits from human review. See the OSSKB terms and license notes in THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md.

docs.title: Generate notice, security & risk reports
docs.text: Beyond SBOM generation, BomLens produces an open-source notice (NOTICE) and a security vulnerability report in one run. This page covers how to generate those outputs. For how to read and interpret them, see What the reports mean.

docs.title: Quick start (5 minutes)
docs.text: If this is your first time, this is all you need. With the Docker engine running, generate the SBOM, notice, and security report in one run — from the browser or the CLI.

docs.title: Browser UI (no command line)
docs.text:
Launch the UI, then enter a project name and version, pick a scan target, run, and download the notice and security report.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --ui     # opens http://localhost:8080 (port taken? UI_PORT=9090 ./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --ui)
#   Windows: double-click scripts\sbom-ui.bat

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
From the project folder you want to scan:

cd /path/to/your-project
/path/to/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project MyApp --version 1.0.0 --all --generate-only

On Windows, use scripts\scan-sbom.bat (Git Bash) or run as-is under WSL2. Installation is in Getting started.

When it finishes, open MyApp_1.0.0/MyApp_1.0.0_NOTICE.html and MyApp_1.0.0/MyApp_1.0.0_security.html to check the results right away — each run's files land together in that MyApp_1.0.0/ subfolder. See below for the detailed options.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker engine 20.10+ (free: WSL2 + docker-ce, or Rancher Desktop / Docker Desktop, which is paid for organizational use)
  • Pull the scanner image: 
    docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest   # the former name sbom-scanner is the same image
  • Run every example from the root of the project to scan.

Output flags are best used together with --generate-only (save locally). Omit it to also auto-upload to an external system (a Dependency-Track server or TRUSCA); pick the target with UPLOAD_TARGET.

docs.title: Generate everything at once (--all)
docs.text:
--all is shorthand for --notice --security --spdx. It produces the SBOM, the notice, the security report, and an SPDX copy of the SBOM in a single scan.

In the web UI and the desktop app the notice and the security report are generation options on the New scan screen, and the SPDX copy is exported from the results screen once the scan is done.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --all --generate-only

Generated files, all together in a MyApp_1.0.0/ subfolder next to where you ran the command (see Where outputs go): 

MyApp_1.0.0_bom.json            # SBOM (CycloneDX 1.6)
MyApp_1.0.0_NOTICE.txt          # notice (text)
MyApp_1.0.0_NOTICE.html         # notice (HTML)
MyApp_1.0.0_security.json       # security report (raw Trivy)
MyApp_1.0.0_security.md         # security report (summary)
MyApp_1.0.0_security.html       # security report (visual)
MyApp_1.0.0_risk-report.md      # open-source risk report (summary)
MyApp_1.0.0_risk-report.html    # open-source risk report (visual)

The open-source risk report (_risk-report) is generated by default in every analysis mode (license + vulnerability tally, with response deadlines). To skip it, use --no-report. For handling each of the seven input forms, see the Scenarios guide.

For the full list of artifact kinds, see the artifacts reference; to generate them from a browser, see the web UI.

docs.title: Open-source notice (--notice)
docs.text:
Gathers the components[].licenses information from the SBOM and generates a notice that groups components by license.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --notice --generate-only
  • _NOTICE.txt — standard text, good to ship with the distribution.
  • _NOTICE.html — a browser-friendly format. All package metadata is HTML-escaped and safe.
  • Components with no license information are classified as NOASSERTION.

For license normalization and full-text bundling behavior, see What the reports mean.

Example (text): 

License: Apache-2.0
Components (1):
  - requests@2.31

docs.title: Security vulnerability report (--security)
docs.text:
Scans the generated SBOM with Trivy and reports known vulnerabilities (CVEs). (NVD + OSV + GHSA DB)

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --security --generate-only
  • _security.json — raw Trivy JSON. For CI or machine processing.
  • _security.md — a per-severity tally table and CVE list. Good to attach to a PR or issue.
  • _security.html — a visual report with severity badges and tables.

The report does not fail the scan even when vulnerabilities exist (report-only). If you need a gate, post-process _security.json.

Trivy matches a component by its package PURL. In a firmware, root filesystem or binary scan, a component that has no package PURL (none, pkg:generic, or one that points at a source repository such as pkg:github) but has a CPE is also matched against the NVD CPE index bundled in the image, and its CVEs are merged into the same report. This covers binaries identified by their version string, such as OpenSSL or BusyBox in an embedded root filesystem with no package database. The index works offline.

A component that no check could reach is not counted as clean. When a component has no version, or has no package PURL and no CPE that was matched, the report says how many there are and lists them under "Components that could not be checked", in place of "No known vulnerabilities found". _security.json keeps the same list as UncheckedComponents (Count, and Components with Name, Version, PURL and Reason: no-version or no-identifier), and the risk report repeats it in its vulnerability section.

A finding that Trivy files under a distribution's advisory number instead of a vulnerability id (a Debian advisory such as DLA-4792-1 or DSA-..., Oracle Linux ELSA-..., SUSE and openSUSE SUSE-SU-... or openSUSE-SU-..., Bottlerocket BRSA-...) is not listed as a vulnerability. Trivy does this when the advisory data names no CVE for the finding; Red Hat, Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux findings already come out under their CVE. When the advisory names a CVE, the finding is reported under that CVE and the advisory number is kept in the CVE's VendorIDs; the web UI shows it next to the CVE id. A CVE that Trivy did not already report for the package takes the advisory's severity and fixed version, not a severity of its own: when several advisories name it, the highest of their severities and all their fixed versions, and it is marked bomlens:fromAdvisory. A CVE counts as named when it is in VendorIDs, or when PrimaryURL or a reference is that CVE's own record page (on nvd.nist.gov, cve.org, cve.mitre.org, or SUSE's CVE page); a CVE that only appears in some other link is not taken. When the advisory names no CVE, the finding moves to the top-level Advisories list in _security.json, with Trivy's own fields (VulnerabilityID, PkgName, PkgIdentifier, InstalledVersion, FixedVersion, Severity, Title) and the Target it came from. These advisories are not counted in the totals or the severity counts, get no EPSS or KEV lookup, and do not trip --fail-on. The security report lists them under "Advisories with no CVE", and the web UI shows them in the security section as a list of their own below the findings.

Every other id stays a finding, including records from vulnerability databases that describe one vulnerability with no CVE (GHSA, GO, PYSEC, RUSTSEC, MAL, OSV, Debian's TEMP and others). A Node.js security working group entry (NSWG-ECO-...) that names a CVE is reported under that CVE in the same way, with its number in VendorIDs; one that names none stays as it is. A lower-case ghsa- or cve- prefix is written in upper case. This is done to Trivy's result before the other engines' results are merged in, so a CVE that another engine also reports for the same package is listed once. When anything is changed, Trivy's unchanged result is kept in _security_trivy.json.

For severity, CVSS, EPSS, and KEV priority signals and follow-up interpretation, see What the reports mean.

docs.title: Deep CVE matching (--deep-cve)
docs.text:
Trivy matches vulnerabilities by package identity (PURL), which covers the ecosystem advisory databases well. Some CVEs in older Java libraries, however, are recorded only in the NVD against a CPE identifier, so a PURL-based scan never reaches them. --deep-cve adds a second pass: BomLens derives an NVD-matchable CPE for each Maven component from its groupId (that enrichment step targets Maven), then grype matches every component's CPE, whatever ecosystem it came from, against a bundled NVD database. In practice most of the extra findings are still Maven, since that is where the enrichment adds a CPE the SBOM did not already carry.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --deep-cve --generate-only
  • --deep-cve implies --security. The extra findings merge into the same security report (_security.json/.md/.html), tagged with their nvd:cpe source.
  • The scan runs on the opt-in ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-deep-cve:latest image, which bundles grype and its database; it is pulled automatically when the flag is set (override with SBOM_DEEP_CVE_IMAGE). It applies to the base-image modes (source, image, binary, rootfs, SBOM analysis); a firmware or AI-model scan prints a warning and runs without grype, since neither produces package purls for it to match. A source scan runs its post-processing step (where the security report is made) on the deep-cve image; when that image cannot be pulled (offline, or SBOM_PULL=never), the source scan goes on without the grype match, says so, and records the deep-cve step as skipped in bomlens-result.json. So it does when SBOM_SCANNER_IMAGE is a local build with no registry path (bomlens:dev), a version before 1.13.2 or not a BomLens image name, and SBOM_DEEP_CVE_IMAGE is not set: no deep-cve image of that build is known, so post-processing stays on the image you named. If that image has grype (built with SBOM_DEEP_CVE=true), the match runs there and is recorded as it came out. The deep-cve image has no scancode, so with --deep-license as well the licence scan runs first in the deep-license image and the post-processing step then runs on the deep-cve image: the run writes both _scancode.json and _security_grype.json. The web UI does the same when it runs from the deep-license image. A first use pulls each opt-in image once, with docker's progress shown; a pull that prints nothing for two minutes is stopped and the scan goes on without that image.
  • In the web UI (and the desktop app), the same option is the Deep CVE matching (NVD CPE) toggle in the scan options. It is offered on every scan mode that uses the base image — source, Docker image, rootfs, package upload, and SBOM upload — and hidden only for firmware and AI-model scans, matching the CLI. Turning it on switches the security report on too, and the deep-cve image downloads once on first use, either as a sibling container or in-process if the UI itself was launched from that image.
  • CPE matching is looser than PURL matching, because NVD version ranges can be recorded coarsely. By default the scan stays offline: such findings are kept and marked version-unverified in the report (a dagger with a footnote), so a reader knows which rows may be loose-version false positives. To tighten them, set SECURITY_NVD_VERIFY=true with an NVD_API_KEY: each finding is then checked against the live NVD version range and out-of-range false positives are dropped. The verification needs network access and adds minutes.
  • For an OS package (rootfs or image scan), the component's cpe carries the plain upstream version; the distro's own package revision (a Debian +deb12u3, an RPM .el9, an Alpine -r0, ...) stays only in its purl and version. A distro that has already backported a fix keeps the same upstream version in its CPE, so a --deep-cve match against NVD's version range can still flag that CVE even though the installed package is patched. The base security report above, which matches by PURL and OS context, already knows the distro's own advisory state and is the one to trust for an OS package's real vulnerability status; read a --deep-cve finding on an OS package the same way as a version-unverified one, as a lead to check rather than a final verdict.
SECURITY_NVD_VERIFY=true NVD_API_KEY="your-key" \
  ./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --deep-cve --generate-only

docs.title: Go reachability (--reachability)
docs.text:
A vulnerability in a Go module matters only when the program uses the affected code. --reachability asks govulncheck, the Go project's own checker, which advisories the scanned Go program actually reaches. For a source tree it follows the call graph from the program's entry points; for a Go executable (--target ./app) it looks for the affected functions in the executable's symbols.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --reachability --generate-only
./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --target ./app --reachability --generate-only
  • Each Go advisory against a component of the SBOM gets a judgement in _reachability.cdx.json, a CycloneDX VEX document. When the affected code is not reached, analysis.state is not_affected and analysis.detail says why. The justification is code_not_present when the affected package is not in the build, and code_not_reachable when it is there but no affected function is called (source) or linked (executable). When it is reached, the state is exploitable and the detail gives the call path or the symbol.
  • The security report shows the not-reachable findings in a section of their own, with the reason, and leaves them out of its totals. Nothing is hidden: the findings are still in _security.json, each marked with bomlens:reachability. A reached finding is marked with a double dagger in the findings table. The risk report and --fail-on vulnerability= count the same way as the security report.
  • --reachability implies --security. It applies to Go source and Go executables; other scans print a warning and run without it. A source scan runs govulncheck inside the Go image of stage 1, which has the Go toolchain; the post-processing image carries only the govulncheck executable.
  • A source scan judges every Go module the SBOM reads, one for each go.mod (up to 20). The modules are found as the SBOM's are: not under vendor/, node_modules/, a folder whose name starts with ., or the non-shipped folders a source scan leaves out (BOMLENS_INCLUDE_NON_SHIPPED=1 keeps them in both). Each module is read for GOOS linux, darwin and windows with GOARCH amd64, and an advisory reached in any module or on any of the three GOOS is exploitable. A module that a go.work lists is read in workspace mode. A module with a vendor/ folder is read from that folder, as the tree was before the scan's go mod tidy; with BOMLENS_KEEP_BUILD_OUTPUT=1 the tree is not put back, so a module outside a workspace is read from the module cache instead (-mod=mod). With more than 20 modules the step is skipped (too_large).
  • A GOOS the module's code does not build for (every file is constrained to other systems, or it uses a field or function only other systems have) is left out for that module and named in the not_affected details and in bomlens:reachability:goos-not-covered; the module is judged from the GOOS that built. A module that builds for none of the three is not judged (bomlens:reachability:modules-not-judged), and the step is recorded as degraded; every module its go.mod requires then gets no not_affected from the other modules' runs (bomlens:reachability:not-affected-withheld), and none is written at all when that go.mod cannot be read. Any other failure of a govulncheck run (a module that cannot be downloaded, a type error on every GOOS, a run over the time limit) fails the step, the runs left are skipped and nothing is written.
  • govulncheck reads the Go vulnerability database (vuln.go.dev) over the network. When it cannot, the step is recorded as skipped (unavailable) in bomlens-result.json and the security report is as without the option.
  • Only the code govulncheck can see is judged. A function called through reflection or from a plugin is not on the call graph, and an executable's symbols show what is linked, not what runs. A source scan reads the files that GOOS linux, darwin or windows (GOARCH amd64) builds with the default build tags: code that only a custom build tag, another GOOS or another GOARCH compiles in is not seen, and neither is code called only from _test.go files (govulncheck leaves tests out by default). The VEX says so in each not_affected detail and in its metadata.properties (bomlens:reachability:goos, goarch, build-tags, modules). Treat not_affected as the tool's judgement and keep an advisory open where the code is loaded in ways the call graph does not show, or where your build sets its own tags.

docs.title: Deep license detection (--deep-license)
docs.text:
The basic notice covers the licenses of dependencies (third-party). --deep-license uses scancode-toolkit to also detect license headers in the project's own source code (first-party).

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --notice --deep-license --generate-only

scancode is heavy and slow (minutes to tens of minutes for a large repo), so it is not in the base image. The CLI runs a source scan's post-process step on the opt-in ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-deep-license:latest image when the flag is set, and pulls it automatically (override with SBOM_DEEP_LICENSE_IMAGE). In the web UI, deep license detection is one of the Generation options and needs the UI itself to run from that image:

SBOM_SCANNER_IMAGE=ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens-deep-license:latest ./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --ui

Only the project's own files are scanned: dependency folders (node_modules, vendor, virtual environments), build output and tool folders are left out, since their licences come from the package managers. A tree with more than 20,000 such files is not scanned, and scancode is stopped after 600 seconds; DEEP_LICENSE_MAX_FILES and DEEP_LICENSE_TIMEOUT change the limits (Docker image environment variables). Either case is noted in the log and in the run's result manifest.

Additional output: MyApp_1.0.0_scancode.json

docs.title: Outbound-license conflicts (--license)
docs.text:
Declares the license you distribute under, so each dependency can be judged against it. A source scan cannot infer this — cdxgen leaves the root license empty for maven and gradle trees — so without the flag no verdict is produced.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --license Apache-2.0 --all --generate-only

The value is recorded on the SBOM's root component, and the risk report gains a conflict section. An existing root license — a supplier SBOM's own declaration — is never replaced. For how to read the verdicts see What the reports mean.

docs.title: Deterministic output (--byte-stable)
docs.text:
Produces a byte-identical SBOM for the same input. It removes meaningless diffs in CI (timestamps, random IDs, ordering differences) and ensures reproducibility.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project "MyApp" --version "1.0.0" --byte-stable --generate-only

What it does: fixes metadata.timestamp to 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, removes the random serialNumber, sorts components by purl, and sorts keys.

docs.title: SBOM signing (--sign)
docs.text:
Creates a detached signature on the SBOM with cosign to establish supply-chain trust. It is offline key-based signing (--tlog-upload=false), so no network or OIDC is needed.

# 1) Generate a key (first time only). For a passwordless key, use COSIGN_PASSWORD=""
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/keys -w /keys -e COSIGN_PASSWORD="" \
  --entrypoint cosign ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest generate-key-pair

# 2) Scan while signing (COSIGN_KEY=private key path, COSIGN_PASSWORD=key password)
COSIGN_KEY="$PWD/cosign.key" COSIGN_PASSWORD="" \
  ./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project MyApp --version 1.0.0 --sign --generate-only

# 3) Verify
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w --entrypoint cosign \
  ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest \
  verify-blob --key cosign.pub --signature MyApp_1.0.0_bom.json.sig \
  --insecure-ignore-tlog MyApp_1.0.0_bom.json

The private key is mounted read-only into the container. Additional output: MyApp_1.0.0_bom.json.sig

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause / fix trivy not installed ... skipping old image. Pull the latest image with docker pull. --deep-license requested but scancode not in image run with the bomlens-deep-license image (the CLI does this for a source scan unless SBOM_SCANNER_IMAGE names an image that is not a BomLens image, a short local name with no registry path, or a version before 1.13.2), or build one with --build-arg SBOM_DEEP_LICENSE=true. Docker is not running in the UI start the Docker engine (Rancher Desktop/Docker Desktop, etc.) and run it again. Many NOASSERTION in the notice the dependencies have no license metadata. Supplement with --deep-license or check manually. Port conflict (--ui) specify a different port with UI_PORT.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A server is not a single source tree. It is an operating system, the application installed on top of it, and libraries that were linked into the binaries during the build. A scan of any one of these misses the others, which is the usual reason a server SBOM ends up incomplete.

This guide treats a server as two layers — the OS and the application — and scans each with BomLens. Keep the layer SBOMs separate — that is the default, and it keeps each one reviewable on its own. Merge them into one product SBOM only when an external system asks for a single file (see Optional: merge into one SBOM).

Layer What it covers Symptom if omitted OS The OS and its installed packages (e.g. CentOS plus everything in the rpm database) OS vulnerabilities missing Application The target application and its package-manager dependencies, direct and transitive Application dependencies missing

Beyond the two layers, statically linked libraries (for example an openssl or liblfds built into the binary) are a blind spot. A package manager does not declare them and the OS package database does not list them, so neither layer's scan finds them. They have to be detected and recorded separately, and missing them is the most common omission — see Static-link libraries below.

One tool, BomLens, produces both layers; only the input changes. The requirement is that the OS, the application, and the static-link libraries are all accounted for — not that they end up in one file.

docs.title: Common setup
docs.text:
Windows: the commands here are for macOS/Linux. See Getting started for the scan-sbom.bat and WSL2 equivalents.

# Docker 20.10+ required. Pull the scanner image once.
docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest

# Keep the script path in a variable, and send every layer's output to one
# shared directory (each still lands in its own {project}_{version}/ subfolder
# under it — see "Where outputs go" in the CLI reference).
SBOM=/path/to/bomlens/scripts/scan-sbom.sh
OUT=/path/to/server-sboms

docs.title: Layer 1 — OS packages
docs.text:
Scan the server's rootfs (the extracted root filesystem) or a container image of it. Syft reads the rpm/dpkg/apk database and records every installed package with a real purl (pkg:rpm/...).

# A rootfs directory:
$SBOM --project mms-relay-os --version 6.10 \
  --target /path/to/server-rootfs \
  --output-dir "$OUT" \
  --all --generate-only

# Or, if the server is packaged as a container image:
$SBOM --project mms-relay-os --version 6.10 \
  --target mms-relay:6.10 \
  --output-dir "$OUT" \
  --all --generate-only

The target must contain the package database. A folder holding only unpacked install files, with no rpm database, yields empty purls and a useless result. Use the real rootfs or image.

docs.title: Layer 2 — Application code and dependencies
docs.text:
Scan the application source after the build. With a package manager (Maven, npm, pip, Go modules, Conan, and others), transitive dependencies resolve automatically.

cd /path/to/app-source
$SBOM --project mms-relay-app --version 2.0.0 --output-dir "$OUT" --all --generate-only

Build first. Scanning before the build or install leaves transitive dependencies unresolved. For a pure CMake/Make application with no manifest, the component list is sparse; add --deep-license to record the first-party source licenses.

docs.title: Static-link libraries (a blind spot of both layers)
docs.text:
Source scanners do not see libraries that were statically linked into a binary, and neither does the OS package database — this is the blind spot the two layers leave. There is no fully automatic path, so combine two approaches.

Analyze the build-output binary or firmware image to catch what tooling can find:

$SBOM --project mms-relay-bin --version 2.0.0 \
  --target /path/to/delivered-binary \
  --output-dir "$OUT" \
  --all --generate-only

For what the scan still misses, record the source and version by hand from the build script — for example the openssl release the build pulls in (openssl 1.1.1za). For a more precise inventory of statically linked components, you can add a binary composition analysis tool as a complementary check.

docs.title: Verify each layer
docs.text:
Keep the per-layer SBOMs (and the static-link SBOM) as they are. Check each one — not a combined file — so a gap is caught where it belongs. Confirm it is well formed and that its components carry real purls.

cd "$OUT"
for bom in mms-relay-os_6.10/mms-relay-os_6.10_bom.json \
           mms-relay-app_2.0.0/mms-relay-app_2.0.0_bom.json \
           mms-relay-bin_2.0.0/mms-relay-bin_2.0.0_bom.json; do
  echo "$bom: $(jq '.components | length' "$bom") components, \
$(jq '[.components[] | select(.purl)] | length' "$bom") with purl"
done

The two counts should be close for each layer. A large gap means many components lack a purl, which usually points to a raw-directory scan or a hand-written entry. Then validate the schema with the CycloneDX validator.

Keeping the layers separate is the default for a reason: a reviewer sees at a glance which layer is missing or where a vulnerability sits, and each layer's dependency graph stays cleanly scoped to that layer.

docs.title: Optional: merge into one SBOM
docs.text:
Merge only when an external system expects a single product BOM (Dependency-Track and TRUSCA both register one BOM per project). --merge combines the layers, dedupes components by purl, and stamps the top-level component with the product name and version.

cd "$OUT"
$SBOM --project mms-relay-server --version 1.0.0 \
  --merge mms-relay-os_6.10/mms-relay-os_6.10_bom.json \
          mms-relay-app_2.0.0/mms-relay-app_2.0.0_bom.json \
          mms-relay-bin_2.0.0/mms-relay-bin_2.0.0_bom.json \
  --generate-only

This writes mms-relay-server_1.0.0/mms-relay-server_1.0.0_bom.json with metadata.component set to the server product, plus the notice and risk report over the merged set. Each component keeps a bomlens:layer property set to the --project of the layer it came from, so you can still filter by layer (jq '.components[] | select(.properties[]?.value == "mms-relay-os")').

The merge preserves each layer's dependencies graph (edges unioned by ref), so the merged BOM keeps its transitive-dependency information and passes the conformance check's transitive-dependency item. Cross-ecosystem bom-ref collisions are rare; identical refs have their dependsOn lists unioned.

docs.title: What makes a server SBOM incomplete
docs.text:
• Hand-written SBOMs. A tool: manual SBOM almost always omits components. Always generate with a tool.
  • pkg:generic components. Use the standard purl types (pkg:rpm, pkg:maven, and so on) so vulnerability matching works.
  • Raw-directory scans with no metadata. Scanning a folder of unpacked install files, with no package database, leaves purls empty and the whole result useless. Target a real rootfs or image.
  • Scanning before the build. Building the SBOM from a pre-build source tree drops transitive dependencies.

docs.title: Using the web UI
docs.text:
The OS and application layers can also run from the web UI ($SBOM --ui). Put the rootfs under the folder where you launch the UI and use the Directory path input, or scan a container image with the Docker image input. Paths outside the launch folder are rejected for safety; to scan a rootfs stored elsewhere, launch the UI with --ui --mount <dir> and the folder appears as a read-only location in the Directory path input. --mount / exposes the running host OS itself the same way (pseudo filesystems such as /proc and /sys are skipped automatically, and results still save under the launch folder). The static-link layer and the optional merge are most direct from the CLI.

Related: Input scenarios | Firmware analysis | Validating a received SBOM | CLI reference

docs.title: Supplier SBOM validation guide
docs.text: How to validate that an SBOM (JSON) received from a supplier or another team meets your quality criteria. After validation, BomLens analyzes the licenses and vulnerabilities and produces a risk report. You only need the SBOM file — no source code required.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it when a supplier or another team hands you an SBOM file instead of source, and you need to confirm the SBOM meets your quality criteria and then check its licenses and vulnerabilities. The input can be CycloneDX (JSON or XML) or SPDX (JSON, Tag-Value); it is converted to CycloneDX internally for analysis. SPDX RDF/XML is not supported yet.

BomLens was built for SK Telecom's supplier SBOM submission, and the table below follows its requirements. The criteria check whether an SBOM is good enough for dependency review. Requirements vary by organization; see SK Telecom's supply chain security guide and its SBOM requirements.

Category Criteria Format CycloneDX v1.3–1.7 or SPDX v2.2–2.3 Required metadata timestamp, tool info, top-level component name and version Required component fields name, version, PURL in standard pkg:type/name@version form, with the namespace the type requires (pkg:maven/<groupId>/<artifactId>, pkg:rpm/<distro>/<name>); a type purl-spec defines, and not pkg:generic Completeness both direct and transitive dependencies included Recommended supplier, license (SPDX ID), hash

The accepted format ranges above are the SK Telecom submission defaults. If your organization accepts a different range, override them with the CYCLONEDX_SPEC_VERSIONS, AI_CYCLONEDX_SPEC_VERSIONS (AI SBOMs), and SPDX_SPEC_VERSIONS environment variables (space-separated lists). They are listed in the Docker image environment variables.

The pkg:generic line above is the skt-submission conformance profile (--conformance-profile skt-submission), not the tool's own default. The default profile treats pkg:generic as advisory instead of a failing requirement and accepts 90% PURL coverage rather than 100%; the web UI's submission-review screen already defaults to skt-submission, but the CLI does not, so pass the flag explicitly when checking against this table.

docs.title: From the web UI
docs.text:
Open the web UI, choose SBOM upload, and upload the file you received; enter a project name and version, then run. A Yocto SPDX 2.2 build hands over an <image>.spdx.tar.zst rather than a document — that archive uploads here too, since it is the only SBOM such a build produces.

If the SBOM leans Java (Maven), turn on Deep CVE matching (NVD CPE) in the scan options. It checks older Maven libraries against NVD-only vulnerabilities that other advisory sources miss, at the cost of a longer scan. It is the same matching as the CLI's --deep-cve; for which scan modes offer the toggle and what the first run downloads, see Deep CVE matching.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --ui     # opens http://localhost:8080
#   Windows: double-click scripts\sbom-ui.bat

Installation is in Getting started.

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
Prefer no command line? See the no-CLI quick start first. What follows is the CLI path.

Pull the scanner image once (docker pull ghcr.io/sktelecom/bomlens:latest), then pass the SBOM file to --analyze:

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project supplier-app --version 2.0.0 \
  --analyze "./supplier-sbom.json" \
  --conformance-profile skt-submission \
  --generate-only

--analyze turns on notice and security analysis automatically, so you do not need to add --all. --generate-only leaves only the outputs in a {Project}_{Version}/ subfolder under the current directory and cleans up the temporary working copy. For the remaining options, see the usage guide.

docs.title: The four outputs
docs.text:
Output File Meaning Conformance check report {Project}_{Version}_conformance.{json,md,html} whether the quality criteria are met, and what is missing SBOM (converted) {Project}_{Version}_bom.json SPDX inputs converted to CycloneDX 1.6; CycloneDX inputs keep their original spec version Open-source notice {Project}_{Version}_NOTICE.{txt,html} components grouped by license Risk report {Project}_{Version}_risk-report.{md,html} conformance, vulnerabilities, and licenses combined, with response deadlines

A self-generated scan produces the same conformance check report file by default too (see Input scenarios), and its summary goes into section 1 of the risk report either way. The pass/fail screen described below, though, only appears on the --analyze path: a self-generated SBOM grading itself is not a meaningful signal for most of its checks. To see it on screen for your own output, feed the generated SBOM back in with --analyze.

docs.title: Reading the conformance check report
docs.text:
The conformance check report is the per-item check of whether the received SBOM meets the quality criteria. Validation is based on the original input before conversion, so even for SPDX it checks the fields of the original SPDX.

  • If any required item falls short, it is a fail. The required items match the criteria table in When to use it — spec version range (CycloneDX v1.3–1.7, SPDX v2.2–2.3), timestamp, tool info, top-level component, name/version coverage, PURL coverage and syntax (standard pkg:type/name@version form, no pkg:generic), the PURL namespace where the type requires one, and transitive dependencies.
  • The namespace check covers every type whose namespace purl-spec marks required, not only OS packages: a pkg:maven identifier without its groupId, or a pkg:rpm identifier that carries the distribution only as a ?distro= qualifier, is well-formed text that resolves to nothing. pkg:golang and pkg:huggingface are reported on a separate advisory row, because an identifier of either can legitimately have no namespace (a Go module path can be a bare host; a model published outside an organization has no owner segment).
  • The top-level component name must name the product. Some generators write a fixed value in its place (., .., / or /scan, the directory they scanned), and SBOMs for different products then collide. Under skt-submission that name fails the "Top-level component name+version" row; under the default profile it warns. Whether the name collides with another submission is for the intake system to decide, and this check cannot see it.
  • Not checked: that a server delivery includes its OS packages, that an OS package's purl names the distribution actually installed (a pkg:deb/debian/... purl on a RHEL server is well formed and passes), and the file basics (extension, size, JSON syntax). Check those with the validation checklist.
  • --resolve-purl adds one more row, and it is the only part of the check that uses the network. It asks each package repository whether the identifiers actually name packages that exist, which catches what no format check can: pkg:maven/org.drools/org.drools.drools-core-dynamic@… repeats its groupId inside the artifactId, and pkg:maven/The%2BApache%2BSoftware%2BFoundation/poi@… carries a vendor display name where the groupId belongs. Both are well formed and both resolve to nothing. The row is advisory and never fails the SBOM: a package published only to an internal repository answers exactly the same way, so set PURL_RESOLVE_IGNORE to the namespaces you know are internal. The coordinate is checked, not the version, because a vendor rebuild version is legitimate and absent from the public repository.
  • The PURL type is checked against the types purl-spec defines. A generator that rebuilds identifiers from a display name can invent one (pkg:applications/java@11.0.25), and nothing else in the report sees it. It warns under the default profile and fails under skt-submission. The list of types lives in docker/lib/purl-types.json. skt-submission also accepts pkg:sourceforge and pkg:gnu, which name a project at its release on SourceForge or the GNU site.
  • Under skt-submission two more rows say what to fix. "Version needed" is required and fails only on components that have neither a version nor a reason. A component whose version the supplier explained with a reason (own-code, not-open-source or version-unknown) is listed under "Explained by the supplier" in the .md and .html report (explained in the JSON), and the row can pass while that list is not empty; under --analyze the list comes from the bomlens:versionReason properties in the supplier's SBOM. "No upstream purl" lists the components that have a version but no purl naming their source repository, as a warning: it is not for the supplier to fix, it does not block the submission, and SK Telecom checks those components separately. For a supplier's SBOM checked with --analyze, the "Version needed" row says to ask the supplier for a corrected SBOM and the "No upstream purl" row to ask for a rescan with a current BomLens; a supplier who scans firmware, a root filesystem or a binary with BomLens fills the versions or reasons in {Project}_{Version}_component-versions.template.csv and scans again with --component-versions (see the firmware guide), and the scan sets the upstream purl for the projects its table covers. For a scan BomLens ran itself, the summary also says that {Project}_{Version}_bom.json is the one file to submit.
  • For a firmware, root filesystem, binary or Yocto build directory scan under skt-submission, the general rows do not fail on what those two rows already cover, and each says why in its detail. Name+version coverage warns when every component missing a version has a reason. PURL coverage warns when every component missing a purl is either explained or versioned (and so listed on "No upstream purl"). "Traceable PURL (no pkg:generic)" warns when every pkg:generic component is a package with a version or a reason. The transitive-dependencies row warns, because such a scan records the packages found, not a dependency graph. None of these rows is relaxed while any component has neither a version nor a reason, or when the SBOM lists no package at all. Such a scan records bomlens:scanMode (FIRMWARE, ROOTFS, BINARY or YOCTO) in metadata.properties, and --analyze judges an SBOM that carries it the same way, saying so in the report summary. A source scan, and any other SBOM under --analyze (from another tool, or from a BomLens version before this marker), keeps these rows as measured. The default profile is unchanged.
  • Your own build outputs have no package repository and so no purl. Listed in a declaration file (--components, or sbom-declared.cdx.json at the scan root) with bomlens:origin first-party, a supplier and a build output in bomlens:artifact (which gives them a SHA-512), they are left out of PURL coverage, "Traceable PURL (no pkg:generic)" and "No upstream purl", and listed by name on the advisory row "First-party components identified by supplier and SHA-512 instead of a purl". This holds only in the scan that read the declaration file: a component marked first-party in an SBOM checked with --analyze still needs a purl, and so does a third-party component in the declaration file.
  • If a recommended item falls short, it is a warn, not a fail. Besides license and hash coverage, this includes the advisory per-component fields the regulatory baselines call for — SHA-512 checksum coverage, component creator, component filename, source/distribution URI, the delivered-file properties (marked review when no scan can see the artifact), and the file component identifier coverage described below.
  • Name/version and PURL coverage are measured over package components only. A binary or firmware SBOM also lists the delivered files as file components, and a file on disk has no package version and no PURL type to carry, so counting them would mark an SBOM short on a field that cannot exist there. Files are still expected to be identified, by the identifier they do carry: the file identifier check measures how many of them have a hash. An SBOM that lists files and no packages at all is a fail, because vulnerability matching keys on package identifiers and a file listing answers none of it.
  • One of the 2026 minimum elements asks the SBOM to say why a field is empty when it is empty — whether the author could not establish the value or is withholding it. An SBOM BomLens generated carries that statement for the whole document, since a scan only ever produces the first case. A received SBOM that says nothing about its absences is reported as a gap on that element.
  • The cards at the top of the HTML report show pass/fail and the list of missing items.
  • Each check that corresponds to a regulatory baseline carries the reference under its row, and a crosswalk section rolls the coverage up per framework — BSI TR-03183-2 (the German technical guideline for the EU Cyber Resilience Act) and the US SBOM minimum elements (2026). The crosswalk is reference material and makes no compliance determination; the AI model SBOM guide describes how it works.

When a fail appears, tell whoever sent the SBOM which fields are missing and ask them to fix it. The most common unmet items are a missing PURL, use of pkg:generic, a PURL built from the component's display name rather than from the package manager (which loses the namespace), and missing transitive dependencies (only direct dependencies included).

docs.title: Reading the risk report
docs.text:
The risk report (_risk-report) is a document built by re-aggregating the outputs above without a new scan. It has four parts.

  1. Requirements met — the conformance results table. If fail, the unmet items are stated.
  2. Vulnerability tally and response deadlines — a severity tally plus the recommended deadlines (a response plan or risk justification within 7 days for Critical and 30 days for High), laid out in a table.
  3. License summary — the notice and license coverage.
  4. Next steps — guidance on a response plan.

docs.title: SPDX input
docs.text: A CycloneDX XML document is rewritten as CycloneDX JSON before validation, keeping component hashes, the root component and the dependency links from it; services, vulnerabilities, pedigree and evidence sections are not carried over, and the scan log names any it skipped. A document that declares a DTD or an entity is refused. If you supply SPDX (JSON, Tag-Value), it is converted to CycloneDX internally with syft convert and then analyzed through the same pipeline. Conformance validation is based on the original SPDX before conversion, because metadata such as timestamp, tools, or transitive dependencies can be normalized away during conversion. Some SPDX license expressions may be simplified when moved to CycloneDX.

docs.title: Yocto images
docs.text:
A Yocto build can produce its own SPDX SBOM, and BomLens reads it with a dedicated parser rather than the generic SPDX path, because a Yocto document carries two things the generic path loses.

To produce one, add the following to local.conf and build as usual.

INHERIT += "create-spdx-3.0"
INHERIT += "vex"

Which SPDX version a release can write is not a choice everywhere:

Release SPDX by default create-spdx-3.0 available 4.0 Kirkstone (LTS) 2.2 no — the class does not exist in this release 5.0 Scarthgap (LTS) 2.2 yes 5.1 Styhead and later 3.0 yes (it is the default)

On Kirkstone the setting above cannot be used; that build writes SPDX 2.2, which is read as described below.

Then point the scan at the build directory. You do not need to know where the build put the SBOM.

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project my-image --version 1.0.0 \
  --target ~/poky/build --generate-only

The build directory is recognized as one, and the image SBOM it published — tmp/deploy/images/<machine>/<image>.rootfs.spdx.json, or tmp-glibc/… on an OpenEmbedded build — is analyzed. The build tree itself is not walked: scanning it as a directory would report sysroots and native build tools that never ship in the image.

When several machines or images were built, the most recently written SBOM is analyzed and all the candidates are listed in the log; pass a specific one with --analyze <file> to choose another. A build that writes its images somewhere else entirely (a relocated DEPLOY_DIR) is not found this way either, so name that document the same way. When all you were sent is the SBOM file, upload it in the web UI or pass it to --analyze.

The web UI reads the same folder: pick it with the Directory input (mount it first with --ui --mount ~/poky/build, or use Add folder in the desktop app) and the detection runs exactly as it does on the command line.

The conformance check report of a build directory scan measures the SBOM the scan writes (<Project>_<Version>_bom.json), which is the file to submit, rather than the build's own document. That SBOM records bomlens:scanMode YOCTO, and under --conformance-profile skt-submission it is judged the way a firmware scan is: it records the packages installed, not a dependency graph. A Yocto document passed to --analyze is judged as it was written.

Because that SBOM is the scan's own, it is completed the way a generated SBOM is. --sbom-author, --supplier and --license (as concluded) are recorded, BomLens is listed as a tool with the build lifecycle phase, and the image keeps the name the build gave it but gets a bom-ref, the --version when the build wrote none, and a dependency on every installed package. A timestamp is written when the build gave none, as the manifests do not. With these three options the bsi-tr-03183-2 rows for the SBOM creator, the dependency graph and the primary component can pass. A Yocto document passed to --analyze on its own is someone else's SBOM and none of this is applied to it.

docs.title: Your own recipes and vendor binaries
docs.text:
The build records every package it installed, your in-house recipes and a chip vendor's binary recipes included, but nothing in it says which of them are yours or who supplied them. Say so in a declaration file and pass it with --components. A component names its recipe (PN, the recipe name without its version) in bomlens:yocto-recipe, not a file path, since the paths differ for every machine and work directory:

{
  "bomFormat": "CycloneDX",
  "specVersion": "1.6",
  "components": [
    {
      "type": "application",
      "name": "media-daemon",
      "supplier": { "name": "Example Corp", "url": ["https://example.com"] },
      "licenses": [ { "license": { "name": "LicenseRef-ExampleCorp-Proprietary" } } ],
      "properties": [
        { "name": "bomlens:origin", "value": "first-party" },
        { "name": "bomlens:yocto-recipe", "value": "media-daemon" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

./scripts/scan-sbom.sh --project my-image --version 1.0.0 \
  --target ~/poky/build --components meta-example/sbom-declared.cdx.json

The declaration goes on every package of that recipe installed in the image (media-daemon and media-daemon-cli, for example). Each keeps the name, version, purl and CPE the build wrote, gets the declared type, supplier, licence (as concluded) and bomlens:origin, and is marked bomlens:declared. The files the SPDX document lists for the package are nested under it with their hashes and file names. Yocto hashes files, not packages: SPDX 3.0 gives SHA-256, and SHA-512 from Yocto 6.1; SPDX 2.2 gives SHA-1 and SHA-256; the manifests give no files. BomLens does not make up a package hash, so under --conformance-profile bsi-tr-03183-2 a SHA-512 or file name the build did not record, and the file properties no Yocto record gives, are reported as not in the source SBOM, a warning. Under skt-submission the first-party exemption from the PURL rows needs a SHA-512, so on a build before 6.1 your packages keep needing a purl (their pkg:yocto purl counts as one without an upstream repository).

The scan fails, naming the recipe, when a declared recipe installed no package in the image; the SBOM written so far is kept as <Project>_<Version>_bom.refused.json. A recipe declaration cannot also give bomlens:artifact, or the hashes, purl or cpe the build decides. A component with neither a recipe nor a file, such as a blob the device loads at run time, is added as in a source scan, unless it has the name of a package the image installs: that one is declared by its recipe.

A package is matched only by the recipe the build recorded for it (in the SPDX document, or in license.manifest for a build without SPDX); one whose recipe was not recorded is not matched by its name, and the refusal names it. A multilib or SDK variant of a recipe (lib32-media-daemon, nativesdk-media-daemon) is a recipe of its own: declare it separately, and the log warns about any the image installs. Declarations apply to the build directory given with --target; --components is refused with --analyze, since an SBOM passed there is received and is not changed. The web UI cannot declare Yocto recipes yet.

The supplier alone can also come from the build. With SPDX 3.0, set it per recipe in your layer and build again:

SPDX_PACKAGE_SUPPLIER_name:pn-media-daemon = "Example Corp"
SPDX_PACKAGE_SUPPLIER_type:pn-media-daemon = "organization"

Yocto writes it as the package's suppliedBy, which BomLens reads as its supplier. It is a name only, with no URL or email (which BSI TR-03183-2 asks of a creator), and it does not mark the package as yours, so the declaration file is still the way to state bomlens:origin. SPDX 2.2 writes SPDX_SUPPLIER, whose default names OpenEmbedded rather than the actual supplier, and BomLens does not read it.

docs.title: A build that produced no SPDX at all
docs.text:
Turning create-spdx on is a build-configuration change, and whoever holds a finished build directory cannot always make one. A build records what it shipped regardless, and those records are read instead:

What Where Gives Image package manifest tmp/deploy/images/<machine>/<image>.manifest the installed packages and their versions License manifest tmp/deploy/licenses/**/license.manifest each package's license and the recipe it came from cve-check report tmp/log/cve/cve-summary.json per CVE, whether a recipe patched it, judged it not applicable, or left it open

This is the weakest of the three inputs, and worth knowing why: there are no CPEs, so vulnerability matching has only names and versions to work with, and the CVE verdicts are only as complete as the build's own cve-check run (a build that never ran it reports no verdicts rather than none existing). The conformance check report measures the SBOM read from these records, as for any build directory scan. Adding the two local.conf lines above and rebuilding remains the better answer.
